speechtext:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: INCREASES IN INTEREST RATES-ALTERNATIVES TO FOLLOWING U.S. INCREASES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister based on his admonition in the Throne Speech debate concerning people, notably myself, who were expressing concern about the future of the economy. He said, and I quote:
-I believe this is a time for Canadians to raise their expectations, not to lower them.
Within two weeks of that-last Thursday-the Prime Minister talked of very tough decisions that he had to take. In three answers on October 25, he used the word "tough" four times. Apparently what he is advocating now is tough decisions that his government has to make, but perhaps even tougher on Canadians than they are on his government.
My question is this: Since, in the view of the government, we have to follow American interest rates up to 11, 12, 13, 14 per cent, at what rate do we begin to look at alternatives? I just remind the Prime Minister that at his press conference on Friday he said:
-given the situation that we face in the economy now, we literally have no alternative except alternatives that will make the situation worse in time to come.
At what point will the government look at these alternatives, rather than following the American interest rate up to 13, 14 per cent and God knows how high?

subsubtopic: INCREASES IN INTEREST RATES-ALTERNATIVES TO FOLLOWING U.S. INCREASES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we are looking at alternatives now. As I have indicated several times in this House, I hope that members of all parties-and, indeed, members of the public-will take advantage of the fact there is now a standing committee inquiry into interest rate policies, to put forward alternative policies they think might be more effective than those which have been proposed by the governor of the Bank of Canada and supported by this government.

subsubtopic: INCREASES IN INTEREST RATES-ALTERNATIVES TO FOLLOWING U.S. INCREASES
speechtext:
The Prime Minister is inviting the public to put alternatives in front of a standing committee. I remind the Prime Minister that on February 13 last, when making a speech precisely on the high interest rates-which I believe then were around 10 per cent-he proposed a number of alternatives. These are recorded at page 3174 of this year's Hansard. I will not read the proposals, but they had to do with currency swaps, borrowing from the IMF, revaluation of Canada's gold reserves, a reduction in the rate of monetary expansion, and raising the chartered bank secondary reserve ratio. He had a whole series of alternatives he was proposing then.
This is the question he asked our minister after proposing these alternatives, and which I now ask the Prime Minister:

October 29, 1979
Oral Questions
When he rises in his place today, will he explain to the people of Canada and to Parliament why these alternatives 1 have listed are not acceptable, whether they are being considered and, if so, whether there is any intention to follow any of them? Can the Prime Minister tell us which of these alternatives that were so brilliantly set out last February he is looking at now.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Solicitor General of Canada
subsubtopic: INCREASES IN INTEREST RATES-ALTERNATIVES TO FOLLOWING U.S. INCREASES
speechtext: What was the answer we got then?

subsubtopic: INCREASES IN INTEREST RATES-ALTERNATIVES TO FOLLOWING U.S. INCREASES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 appreciate the Leader of the Opposition's retrospective description of my proposals at that time as brilliant. 1 will have to refresh my memory. I believe those remarks were made in relation to policy having to do with the value of the Canadian dollar. I can review the record.
The fact is that we are, and have been, reviewing various alternatives since we were elected as a government. Our judgment, which confirms the view of the governor of the Bank of Canada, is that the most appropriate policy for the Government of Canada to follow, now, is to follow the advice put forward by the governor of the Bank of Canada. He stated his reasons for giving that advice. The Minister of Finance will be stating again his reasons for following that advice.
We continue to welcome any suggestions that might come from anywhere in the country, including the official opposition, as to policies that will work, that should be considered and that might be preferable alternatives.

subsubtopic: INCREASES IN INTEREST RATES-ALTERNATIVES TO FOLLOWING U.S. INCREASES
speechtext:
The Prime Minister says that he is now following these policies. I recall quite distinctly that when we were following those policies, it was seen as a sign of abject servility to the United States.
In what sense does it take more courage now to apply those policies, when we have already gone up to 14 per cent? They might have been appropriate at 7 or 8 per cent, but surely at some point one begins to look at new policies. Since the Prime Minister listed a whole ream of them, 1 would like to know which ones the government is looking at, and why they have been discarded.

subsubtopic: INCREASES IN INTEREST RATES-ALTERNATIVES TO FOLLOWING U.S. INCREASES
speechtext:
1 am pleased the Leader of the Opposition can remember when his party was following those policies, because his finance critic is doing his best to forget.
The right hon. gentleman has made a very valuable suggestion. It may be we have not examined each one of the proposals I put forward in February as closely as we should. We have reviewed certain of those policies. I will go back and read my speech again and see whether there are any suggestions we should be looking at more assiduously than has been the case.
I repeat, we feel it highly important that, in the circumstances this country faces today, we need to call on all Canadians with proposals for a better approach than the one that has been criticized by the Leader of the Opposition. If they can come up with a better proposal than the one we are following, we will consider it. But having looked at the alterna-

fives, our judgment is-and this is also the judgment of the governor of the Bank of Canada-that the policies recommended by the governor, even though they are tough, even though they are not popular, are the best policies available.

subsubtopic: INCREASES IN INTEREST RATES-ALTERNATIVES TO FOLLOWING U.S. INCREASES
speechtext: Why is the Prime Minister trying to get the Canadian people to forget that when he was speaking as Leader of the Progressive Conservative Party, he said a Progressive Conservative government would bring interest rates down? What is wrong with that policy today? It was all right when he spoke on March 2. Why is he abandoning it today?

subsubtopic: INCREASES IN INTEREST RATES-ALTERNATIVES TO FOLLOWING U.S. INCREASES
speechtext: The goal of our policy is to bring interest rates down. That will not be done if we duck tough decisions today. We are facing tough decisions today dealing with interest rates as a means of creating the kind of stability and strength in the economy which will allow us honestly and with some security to bring interest rates down in the future.

subsubtopic: INCREASES IN INTEREST RATES-ALTERNATIVES TO FOLLOWING U.S. INCREASES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: INCREASES IN INTEREST RATES-ALTERNATIVES TO FOLLOWING U.S. INCREASES
speechtext:
It was reported today that officials of the U.S. Federal Reserve Board have disclosed that another $800 million error has been discovered in the monetary supply of that country, in addition to the $3 billion mistake discovered last week. Representative Henry Reuss, chairman of the House of Representatives Banking Committee has called the miscalculation of the money supply "a monumental goof equivalent to a monetary Three-Mile Island."
How can the government continue to justify supporting a policy of following American interest rates so closely, to what are record levels in Canada, when the soundness of the basis of the American policy has been called into question by U.S. experts? Why does the government not act now to prevent our economy from becoming another Three-Mile Island?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister of Finance):
subsubtopic: INCREASES IN INTEREST RATES-ALTERNATIVES TO FOLLOWING U.S. INCREASES
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman is a slow learner. Last year, in 1978, his government approved interest rate increases of 3.25 per cent. This year, to date, we have had to approve increases of the same amount, for several reasons. Among them is that interest rates in the United States have increased this year, and despite the mistake in the calculation of the money supply in the United States the fact remains that interest rates went up in the United States, they were higher in the United States than in Canada, and that even today the prime rate in the United States has gone to 15.25 per cent: Citibank increased their rate on Friday to 15.25 per cent, higher than the prime rate in Canada.
So whether or not a mistake was made in the calculation of the money supply in the United States is irrelevant. The fact is that their interest rates are higher than ours, so to protect our dollar and to stop the surge of inflation which would affect us here in Canada if we did not do so, we had to raise our rates too. The hon. member for St. Moritz understands that-

subtopic: FIGHT AGAINST INFLATION-EFFECT ON STANDARD OF LIVING
FIGHT AGAINST INFLATION-EFFECT ON STANDARD OF LIVING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, reluctant as I am to interrupt the internecine conflict between tight money's first team and tight money's second team, I would like to address a question to the Prime Minister.
Mr. Volcker, who is chairman of the Federal Reserve Board in the United States, has said that the standard of living of the average American has to decline if inflation is to be fought in the United States. 1 wonder if the Prime Minister is going to come clean with the Canadian people and make a statement as to what is going to happen to the standard of living of the average Canadian, and what he is going to do about it in his fight against inflation.

subtopic: FIGHT AGAINST INFLATION-EFFECT ON STANDARD OF LIVING
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, what we are interested in doing in our fight against inflation is taking steps now which will ensure that in the long term the standard of living of Canadians across the country is one which is as high as possible and as reliable as possible. The hon. member knows, and I am sure he is concerned about, the particularly difficult conditions which are imposed, particularly on low income Canadians, by present circumstances. Those circumstances also worry this government very much, and they are circumstances with which we hope to deal in a budget.

subtopic: FIGHT AGAINST INFLATION-EFFECT ON STANDARD OF LIVING
speechtext: When, next year?

subtopic: FIGHT AGAINST INFLATION-EFFECT ON STANDARD OF LIVING
speechtext:
We now have inflation running at 9.6 per cent, and we have projections-but the government is not prepared to tell us exactly what it is going to do-that the price of energy will be going up substantially in order to face certain problems.
How much unemployment, and how much of a reduction in the standard of living over the short term-because we live over the short term, not over the long term-is this government prepared to tolerate in its so-called trench warfare against inflation?

subtopic: FIGHT AGAINST INFLATION-EFFECT ON STANDARD OF LIVING
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as little as possible.

subtopic: FIGHT AGAINST INFLATION-EFFECT ON STANDARD OF LIVING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, governor Bouey said that a rise in interest rates discourages borrowing and spending, and that slower economic growth is the price we all have to pay in the fight against inflation. Instead of talking about biting bullets and making tough decisions, and instead of talking like Superman and acting like Clark Kent, I think it is time the government gave us some figures and an understanding as to what the cost of the government's policy will be both in the energy field and in the interest rate field, and as to how the government intends to distribute these costs to the Canadian consumer-because it is the little guy who is getting screwed by the government's policy.

subtopic: HIGH INTEREST RATES-RENEGOTIATION OF MORTGAGES CAUSED THEREBY
HIGH INTEREST RATES-RENEGOTIATION OF MORTGAGES CAUSED THEREBY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I have a question for the Minister of Finance. By this time, the Minister of Finance must be aware that as a consequence of the high interest rate policy of his government, thousands of Canadian families are facing the horrendous prospect of renegotiating their mortgages at a time when rates have gone up anywhere from 30 per cent to 50 per cent. To put it in other terms, where mortgage rates have gone up, carrying costs have risen as much as $1,500 a year.
Under those circumstances, and now that the Prime Minister has agreed it is time to review policies, is the Minister of Finance also prepared to agree that it is time he took some action to relieve those hardships? In particular, is he prepared to give directives to banks and lending institutions that they provide short-term loans for people caught in those circumstances?
More importantly, is he prepared to provide some shortterm, emergency assistance or low-rate mortgages to enable people to carry over until those great halcyon days when interests rates may go down?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister of Finance):
subtopic: HIGH INTEREST RATES-RENEGOTIATION OF MORTGAGES CAUSED THEREBY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are very conscious of the fact that when interest rates go up, someone suffers. Therefore, we are hoping that the interest rate increase will be as short term as possible.
I am also aware that we are introducing into the House a mortgage interest and property tax credit plan which, if this House passes it before Christmas, will better enable 3,800,000 home owners in Canada to bear the increased costs of mortgage interest, the increased costs of looking after a home, increases in property taxes, or whatever. They will be in a considerably better position to do that if we pass this legislation as quickly as possible. I point out to the hon. member that 76 per cent of Canadians support the mortgage proposal, as shown by a Gallup poll reported in the Toronto Star on October 20. So 1 move that we help that 76 per cent as quickly as possible.

ALLEGED CHANGE IN GOVERNMENT POLICY TO CURB INFLATION-REASON FOR LONG RECESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the right hon. Prime Minister. Since the credibility of this government has been grossly undermined by the reversals in policy since the last election, and since the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance have repeatedly stated that they were not aware of the state of the Canadian economy until they had fully assumed office, would the Prime Minister be specific and tell the House exactly what economic factors have caused him to continue his flip-flop policy?

subsubtopic: ISRAEL-TABLING OF INTERIM REPORT ON LOCATION OF CANADIAN EMBASSY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 would ask the permission of the House to lay upon the table a copy of an interim report in both official languages from the hon. Robert L. Stanfield, special representative of the Government of Canada and ambassador at large.
[ Translation]

Mr. Speaker, I tabled a preliminary report to government by the hon. Robert L. Stanfield, special government representative and ambassador at large on the subject of the location of the Canadian Embassy in Israel.


As part of his mandate, Mr. Stanfield was asked for a recommendation on the implementation of our policy on Jerusalem in a way that would be compatible with the efforts that are being made to achieve a comprehensive peace settlement in the Middle East.
As a result of extensive consultations, Mr. Stanfield has concluded that a change in the location of the Canadian embassy in Israel could be seen as pre-judging negotiations among parties in the Middle East and might, in fact, work against progress to a just and lasting peace settlement.
The purpose of this government is to encourage that peace. Consequently, the government accepts the recommendation that no action be taken on the location of the Canadian embassy until the status of Jerusalem is clarified within a comprehensive agreement between Israel and its Arab neighbours.
We look forward, sir, to receiving Mr. Stanfield's final report so that the government might consider other matters involving our relations with the Middle East.
Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, what we seem to have now is the latest instalment in the series of withdrawals and flip-flops which were alluded to by the hon. member for Stormont-Dundas (Mr. Lumley) today. 1 do not suppose he knew he would be getting this recent instalment today. I must say, however, it is no surprise to the country and to Parliament that this had to come.
This is a very laconic and brief statement and I commend the Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) for making it now, as soon as he received Mr. Stanfield's interim report. When you are going to reverse your position I suppose the best thing is to do it quickly and quietly and sit down, as the Prime Minister has done.
It would have been interesting for Parliament to know why this policy, which is judged to be misguided now, was really adopted in the first place. Did the Prime Minister really think he was helping the cause of peace in the Middle East? We recall that last January when he was visiting that area he said it would be a misguided policy. By the month of April he had changed his mind. Did he change his mind really because he thought he was helping the cause of peace? Did he think he was improving relations with the Middle East? Did he think he was making the job easier for the Canadian peacekeepers in that area? If so, why did he change his mind now? After all, Mr. Stanfield's mission was, in the Prime Minister's own words, "To find recommendations on the way to implement" that policy. We find that now Mr. Stanfield is recommending, not ways to implement it, but clearly a withdrawal from that policy.
The question Canadians must ask the government is: was this really a considered policy by the government? What did it cost? I do not mean only in terms of economic loss, which the Minister of State for International Trade (Mr. Wilson) has
October 29, 1979

told us about, not only millions lost in real contracts but perhaps billions lost in terms of expectations. What did it cost in terms of Canada's credibility in the world?
Hear, hear!

Did it really call for an extensive tour by the right hon. member's former leader of all these various countries to find out that the policy was wrong, that it was misguided? He had been told that not only by members on this side and other parties, he had been told that by his own department. Why did he not change his mind sooner, Mr. Speaker, if there was going to be this loss of credibility, loss of face and this loss of financial considerations?
More important, and what the House would like to know, is what was the price paid to try and save the right hon. Prime Minister's face and that of his party? What price did Mr. Stanfield pay? 1 think we are beginning to see that there was a heavy price to pay, not only for Canada, once again in prestige and economic terms, but a price which was paid by this government in terms of reversing its policy on the move from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem. This is a policy which the government of Israel was justified in believing was made in sincerity, with an intent to carry it out and with the consequent weakening of our relations with a friendly foreign country. Not only, therefore, had Mr. Stanfield the price to pay of saying that he would get his Prime Minister to change that policy, but he also had to pay a much higher cost than that, Mr. Speaker.
I think we had the evidence on Thursday, when we were debating the anti-boycott legislation in this House, that Mr. Stanfield obviously gave another commitment on behalf of the government. The Liberal member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan) presented a bill which was talked out. This was a bill bringing in anti-boycott legislation, a bill which the House will remember was not passed last spring because the government side, which was then in opposition, refused to give unanimous consent to proceed in one day. We were told on Thursday by the hon. member for Burlington (Mr. Kempling), a spokesman for the Conservative government, as reported in Hansard at page 613, that:
-it is our intention to talk this bill out today because we believe the report to be presented by Mr. Stanfield will have an impact-
I suggest that that is the second price paid, Mr. Speaker; not only a withdrawal of the policy of moving the embassy and the consequent embarrassment and disappointment of our friends in Israel, but also the second price, a more serious one, of talking out anti-boycott legislation which could have been passed had that government not deliberately decided to talk it out in the name of some future pie in the sky in the New Year, we are told. But, Mr. Speaker, if the right hon. Prime Minister is sincere in saying that they want to do something in the New Year, nothing would have prevented their coming in with some different kind of legislation. I am sure the House would have given unanimous consent if the hon. Prime Minister would have wanted to improve that legislation, but at least we would
Canadian Embassy in Israel
have something now. So that is the second serious cost of this prime ministerial blunder.
I see you are impatient, Mr. Speaker, because the right hon. Prime Minister did not have much to say, but I think the House has a lot to say on this.
Hear, hear!

1 think the most serious price of all paid by the Hon. Robert Stanfield is the apparent commitment he gave, and the carrying out of that commitment, to meet the PLO. There was no hint from the government that they were going to recognize the PLO. The government, in an answer to the hon. member for Saint-Denis (Mr. Prud'homme), lamely tried to explain that it was not really a recognition of the PLO by the government because somehow Mr. Stanfield was an ambassador extraordinary; presumably he was not representing the government when he talked to the PLO, but presumably he was when he was talking to the other countries. This new theory of international law has never really been explained by the Prime Minister. But I think from the point of view of Israel and the people in Canada who are sympathetic to Israel, the de facto recognition of the PLO by this government as a price paid by the Hon. Robert Stanfield to cover up the right hon. Prime Minister's blunder is a very serious price indeed, I think one which will have lasting effect on the relations of Canada with the Middle East.
Hear, hear!

I can only conclude that this series of reversals is a further indication of the government's incompetence in the matter of foreign affairs. Since there was a reversal between January and April and now another reversal between April and October, I wonder if the information I have received from a high official in one of these Arab countries is not correct when he reported the Hon. Robert Stanfield as having said to some of these governments, "Don't worry, we will change the policy but also we will change the Prime Minister pretty soon".
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, the question of the possibility of moving the Canadian embassy to Jerusalem has to have been one of the most serious decisions- and I will come to that in a minute-and possibly one of the most serious reversals that this government has been involved in since May 22.
Our position as a party has been very clear on this issue. Not only do we see the very legitimate and real interests of the people of Israel and the historical claims of Jews to the city of Jerusalem; we have also recognized the very profound historical, religious and current political claims of the Arab countries. It is by no means a one-sided case that can be made about the fate of Jerusalem. Therefore, we took the position in the election campaign that it was an irresponsible action. In the context of jeopardizing very serious peace negotiations it was possible for the Government of Canada, or for a candidate

October 29, 1979
Canadian Embassy in Israel
at that time for the prime ministership of Canada, to suggest that we would move our embassy unilaterally when the Camp David agreement between the two most important nations directly affected, Egypt and Isreal, had specifically said that the future of Jersualem was something to be resolved later on between the Israelis and the Arabs. We think it was a promise made irresponsibly in the campaign and repeated irresponsibly after the election.
It seems to me that we cannot simply pass these things off with the acknowledgment that an error has been made. I think responsible politics presumes that if you do not have enough information or knowledge about a position, then you do not announce a decision. That is that.
Hear, hear!

It seems to me that the Progressive Conservative leader, now Prime Minister (Mr. Clark), made an irresponsible commitment involving a lot of emotional responses from a good many people of Canada, namely the Jewish community, and for understandable reasons. A good number of them thought this was a positive move. For equivalent reasons a good number of Arab Canadians had contrary views, and certainly the Arab states expressed that view as well.
I want to stress that a good deal of attention has been paid in Canada to the economic reaction. I want to underscore that the Arabs have a religious, political and historical claim that is as profound as the Jews, and it has to be recognized as legitimate. I want to say it was an irresponsible decision to make it an election campaign promise and it was even more irresponsible to carry it out in the days immediately following the campaign.
Having said that, I will come to the Prime Minister's position because I am not yet perfectly clear about it. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Trudeau) may be, but if one reads the Prime Minister's statement it certainly needs some clarification for me.
Mr. Stanfield in his report is unequivocal on the point. He made the recommendation that: "It is my view the question"- please note the words-"of the relocation of the embassy must await the resolution of Jerusalem's status as part of a just and lasting comprehensive peace settlement". He said that after pointing out that the Arabs have "vital religious and political interests", as well as the Israelis.
Mr. Stanfield's position is clear. It seems to me to be the kind of position that every thinking Canadian who did not have profound, expert knowledge but elementary knowledge in the spring would have taken.
I turn to the Prime Minister's statement today, and that is what causes me concern. Unlike Mr. Stanfield, who says that the resolution of the question of the relocation has to be left to the future to be determined ultimately by a settlement reached by the states involved there, the Prime Minister used very different words in his statement. He said that "consequently the government accepts the recommendation that no action" be taken on the location of the Canadian embassy, etc. Maybe

the Prime Minister will clarify this in the time we have to pose questions and receive answers. Why did he not say no decision will be reached now, no decision to move or not to move, until after the future is resolved? The implication at least is that the Prime Minister is holding to his old commitment that at some point a move will take place. If he had chosen the words of Mr. Stanfield, any possible ambiguity would have been removed.
Mr. Stanfield made it clear that the whole question of a move, even at some time in the future, has to be made in the context of a settlement reached by the states in the Middle East. I want to stress that my party is in full agreement with that position. It is in full agreement with Mr. Stanfield's position on this.
In conclusion, while it is clear that the future position about our embassy in the state of Israel, namely its location, has to be left until the future of Jerusalem is in fact determined by the states in the area, I wish to underscore the rights of the Jewish community in Canada to put as much pressure as any other group on the Government of Canada for what they believe in. That is very important.
I want to take this opportunity to dissociate my party from the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Trudeau), who said vis-avis the Jewish community that they have "opened the way to growing anti-Semitism"-and that is from the Leader of the Opposition in the House of Commons-because of the pressure they are putting on the Government of Canada. I want to say the Jews of Canada have the same right as anyone else to push as forcefully as they wish, as forcefully as any Canadian citizen, for any policy they want, whether the Government of Canada ultimately agrees with it. To suggest the contrary is to indulge, or seem to indulge, in the course of action to which the Leader of the Opposition was objecting. I hope he reconsiders his words.

Mr. Speaker, I understand that under the rules we may now ask questions. I must take great exception to the statement by the leader of the New Democratic Party. It is a question of privilege on which I will ask Your Honour's guidance as to when it should be raised. However, I want to say now that he was presumably quoting from some press report which was not quoted accurately. It was not even given in an interview, but at a background briefing; in short, an interview in which I was asked about the actions of Mr. Moshe Dayan.
It is just as unfair for the leader of the New Democratic Party to take it out on me now when he knows I do not have a right under the rules to answer for perhaps a press release issued by some other members of the Canadian community. If the leader of the NDP had a point to make which is not on this particular policy, he should have chosen another way to make it.
My question to the Prime Minister is simply this. I indicated at the beginning of my remarks that Mr. Stanfield had a mandate to say how we could implement the government's
October 29, 1979

policy. We hear now that implementation is not proceeding. The question 1 have for the Prime Minister is: has the policy been changed or is it merely the implementation of it which has been delayed?
Mr. Speaker, it is not our intention now to move the Canadian embassy in Israel to Jerusalem.

Mr. Speaker, I think the word "now" is very, very crucial. I take it, and the Prime Minister can answer me, that the policy has not been changed, that they still want to move the embassy from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem, but they will not do it now. These are the words he used; I ask the Prime Minister to clarify them.

Excuse me, Mr. Speaker, what I should have said is "it is not now our policy". We do not intend to move the embassy from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem. If there is a just and lasting peace settlement that settles and clarifies the question of Jerusalem, that may allow us to reopen the question. Until there is such a clarification within the context of a just and lasting peace settlement, the Canadian embassy will stay in Tel Aviv.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1979-80 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY FOR 1979-80
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that spontaneous outburst by my colleague from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) reminds me of a 90 years old gentleman visiting here from Britain a few days ago who was shocked when he heard everybody clapping; he wondered what had happened to the Canadian Parliament and its following of the tradition of the British house where nobody is ever heard to clap.
October 29, 1979

The reason I participate in this debate is that along with a lot of other Canadians 1 am concerned by the fact that we are going outside the country once again to borrow very large sums of money, in this case about $7 billion, knowing full well that if we did not have a trade balance that carried a deficit of about $8 billion we would probably not have to borrow that money.
In the second place, like anyone who has to go to Household Finance we are going to find as a people that the interest rate is likely to be disastrous, that we will have to pay at least the prime interest rate, probably more, and that part of the reason we are paying it is because the Americans cannot add. It is really extraordinary that the governor of the Bank of Canada should appear before the finance committee and tell us we have to raise our prime rate because the Americans raised theirs, only for the public to find that the Americans raised their interest rate because they had made a mistake in their calculation of the money supply in their country.
So, Mr. Speaker, if 1 go to Household Finance for money to buy a television set, 1 have to suffer because of the inability of some people in America to do arithmetic. It seems idiotic that I should have to pay for a mistake the Americans made. We talk about Canadian identity. Surely our financial structure has not got much if we depend on another country to do the proper calculations and come up with the appropriate interest rate 1 should pay on money I borrow to buy a television, a car, or whatever else 1 might buy in my own country. I believe most Canadians, like myself, disagree with the proposition that we must become continental in setting the price of our money, interest rates, the price of oil, of cars, and of almost every other commodity we use just because the American set it.
The government is now proposing to borrow this money knowing full well we are not following the philosophy of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Crosbie) urging privatization, because privatization, he believes, is the best way of doing things. This philosophy goes out of the window. There is no competition among the banks. We do not find one bank charging one price and another bank charging another. Once a decision is made by the Bank of Canada, all the banks raise their interest rates to the same rate because they all borrow from the same source. All these banks are making a good profit and some of them could probably afford to drop by half a per cent the amount they charge on their loans for houses, farms and so on with a little push from us. That would be possible and they still would be able to make a profit. But they have no intention of doing so. They decide, as a great monopoly, that everybody has to pay the same, no matter what bank they go to.
It is not without interest that some of the staff of the House of Commons have recently decided that they will no longer deal with ordinary banks. Many of the staff in this building have decided to put their money into the Province of Ontario Savings Office. I have never heard of it before myself, but it has a small branch on Sparks Street. The reason they give for doing so is that though there are no frills, no big buildings, there are no extra charges, they get the interest on their money
Borrowing Authority
and if they want to write cheques against the whole of the amount in their account it does not cost them extra. 1 do not know whether the Province of Ontario Savings Office is making a huge profit or not, but even that does not constitute real competition.
The other day we got into a discussion with the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Industry (Mr. Huntington). It was an interesting discussion and I may have missed some of it, but I am not sure why he made an interjection. He did so after 1 had stated that according to the advertisements put out by the pulp and paper companies we should not burn down the forests of Ontario, because in Ontario out of every dollar that changes hands in the province, 27 cents comes directly or indirectly from the forest industry.
Apparently the minister disagreed with that statement. According to him, the major factor in the Canadian economy was the manufacturing sector. Well, Mr. Speaker, he has only been minister for a very short time and he probably does not know much about the situation yet. I listened to him debating on television with the former minister of industry, trade and commerce and I think he ought to take a few lessons before he starts lecturing anyone else.
I was surprised to find that the primary industry is not the big producer in Canada I thought it was. but neither is the manufacturing industry. According to Statistics Canada, the manufacturing industry dropped from 26 per cent in 1970 to 19 per cent now in terms of our gross national product. Its production is going down, not the other way, and this is very much reflected in the deficit we have in our estimated balance of payments for this year, which will be about $8 billion. That figure may increase before the end of the year.
Surprisingly enough, the largest sector in this country is the third sector, the service industry. More transactions take place in that industry, and it is in that industry that the largest percentage of the gross national product is involved. Its production is considerably greater than that of the manufacturing industry of this nation, and it is also much greater than that of the primary industry.
If we want to eliminate our $8 billion estimated balance of payments deficit-and I am sure the minister would like to do that-there is a way of doing it. In this country today we are producing about 1.5 million ounces of gold. That gold was produced by the same mines at about $35 an ounce not too long ago, and the government was subsidizing $15, $20 and up to about $55 an ounce. On the average the country lost about $15 on the gold it was subsidizing, but it is interesting to note that at the end of the emergency gold mines assistance program Canada held enough gold and the increase in the price of gold was sufficient that we were able in one swoop and with a very small amount of gold to write off the total deficit of emergency gold mines assistance. The amounts over 15 years were considered sufficient to keep the mining industry in operation.

October 29, 1979
Borrowing Authority
Not long ago the Ontario government, the federal government and the municipalities involved participated in the Kirkland Lake area in a magnetometer survey, an electronic survey involving ground evaluation and magnetometer and electromagnetic surveys. As a result the maps for that area now show that there is considerably more wealth in the ground in the Kirkland Lake area than has been mined.
If the Minister of Finance was to decide to mine gold again, he would have to mine only 20 million ounces a year to eliminate the balance of payments deficit. Gold is being mined today in the mines which are already in operation. According to estimates the cost of production is about $115 an ounce. That gold is now selling for something over $400 Canadian. If we were to take 20 million ounces plus the cost of production, we could wipe out the total trade deficit we have, the whole balance of payments deficit, for the next year. This is possible. The government would have to make the decision that it would be its development and that it would mine the gold for the specific purpose of getting rid of the balance of payments. It would mean that we would not be out borrowing in the market. We would not be out looking for loans in the countries of the world, including the United States and Europe. We would be able to balance our payments through the simple operation of mining gold.
When we talked about the gold bullion coin, immediately the people in the Department of Finance tore out their hair because of all the work they had done on the Bretton Woods Agreement. 1 understand that we are going to discuss the Bretton Woods Agreement shortly. The Bretton Woods Agreement was drawn up after the war to get rid of the gold standard. It resulted eventually in the establishment of the International Monetary Fund. It was decided that the base of international currency was to be the American dollar. A new unit of borrowing was established. That meant that United States banks lent so much money around the world that if those loans were called, there would be bankruptcies. It is interesting to know that the federal reserve in the United States is smaller than the loan to one country, Turkey. Turkey owes American banks $13 billion. The federal reserve fund is only $9 billion. If the banks were to call that particular loan, obviously the federal reserve fund would be bankrupt. That would mean that the banks in the United States would start to fall because the only thing propping them up is the federal reserve insurance.
That will not happen because the secretary of state and the secretary of defence in the United States will not allow that to happen. If Turkey was put into bankruptcy, Turkey would no longer be in the NATO camp. Therefore, there obviously will not be any effort to collect that loan. In fact, the American people will eventually pay off the loan for defence purposes. The International Monetary Fund did not work. It was set up by people like the minister in charge of small business. They really did not understand the whole problem or its ramifications. They really believed that people would be able to trade on script forever. That meant that the United States was able to print money like it was going out of style, to the point where
[Mr. Peters.)
Nixon, when he was president of the United States, had to declare that there would no longer be a reclaiming of American dollars for gold. When he said that the reclaiming of those bills for gold could no longer be done, that meant that those dollars would never be back in the United States and would in effect be floating around in Europe to be used for whatever purpose the Europeans desired.
It is very interesting to note that those Eurodollars which probably carried an actual value of six cents or seven cents on the dollar were used not long ago by the Reichbank in Germany to buy all the gold that the United States put on the market. The Reichbank bought the total amount, and it would not have mattered what the price was. The bank could have paid $500 or $600 an ounce, it really did not make any difference, because the gold was worth something. The paper was hardly worth the cost to print it.
The Minister of Finance is obviously not going to consider the mining of gold. He is not going to recognize the interest in gold because in financial circles it is considered to be a disaster to look at a base in gold today. However, he really should look at how some countries have balanced their payments. We sell our wheat to Russia. Until very recently Russia has paid us with gold, and we bought that gold at $35 an ounce when gold was selling on the open market at considerably higher prices. Now Russia is asking a number of countries to bid on supplying their currencies against gold on the international market. That will mean that Russia will be selling its gold for acceptable currency with which Russia can buy commodities from other countries, such as our wheat, and give us in return the currencies of other countries.
The reason the Russians have not played around with transferring roubles to Canada and establishing the value of the rouble was very simple. They did not want to debase their own currency. They did not want to put their currency against that of any country in the world. For years they have mined gold and used it as their method of external exchange and foreign trade. They have not played around with the rouble on international money markets. This means, of course, that whatever the value of the rouble, it is not devalued by putting it against any other currency in the world. South Africa has mined gold at great cost, I am sure. I am sure that they have mined gold at a considerably higher price than the $35 they were getting two years ago for that commodity. They mined it simply because they could go to the international marketplace and buy the goods, services and all their needs in such a way as to balance their trade with the gold they produced.
I am sure that we in this country are in a position to produce very easily the 20 million ounces of gold which we would need to balance our payments so that we do not end up with a deficit and have to borrow money. Any sensible government would take means to protect its economy. For instance, one could stop the flow of money out of the country. It was very interesting to read in a U.S. paper that the Americans are very concerned about the control which Canadians have on their
October 29, 1979

money supply. Most people do not realize that we send out more money than we bring into this country. We own many of the financial institutions in the United States through our control of insurance companies. We are the best savers in the world. When we are at the height of prosperity we still prepare for a depression. When people save, they save themselves into a depression. Much of this is done by sending our money out of the country through insurance companies and depositing it in another country at its face value, to be used by that country, such as the United States. We allow Americans to use the inflationary period to reap the benefits of that money, and we are still covered for the face value of the insurance policy which we bought when our dollar was worth $1 rather than the 40 cents or 50 cents it is now worth.
We are probably not going to mine gold, but I would like the minister to look at this question because I am sure he has some new ideas. 1 am sure he is well aware of the fact that the mining industry is perturbed by the fact that gold is not being mined. One of the reasons they cannot mine gold is that an immense outlay of capital is necessary for any mining company to go into operation today, not so much for underground mining because in many cases the mines are there, the reserves are known and so are the values. Samples have been taken and diamond drilling has been done. All possible ways have been explored to ascertain the value of that mine. In fact, all these things have been done in general years ago. But one of the expenses will be the building of a mill, and to make that kind of expenditure, it is necessary for the government to step in.
1 am glad to see the Minister responsible for DREE (Mr. MacKay) here. Perhaps the minister will have to give some consideration to providing a long range financing structure for the establishment of mills. I see in this country the establishment of a big mill in a mining community, the establishment of a custom mill, and the government would be the only entity which the mining community would trust because it is generally believed by the mining community that all mining companies cheat. I worked in the gold mining industry for I 5 years as an underground miner and 1 also agree that generally mining companies cheat and are dishonest. They have nothing to recommend them. Of course, that can be corrected. They do not trust each other, and certainly I did not trust them when 1 was a miner. 1 struck against them many times. 1 did not believe their financial statements because I figured they were loaded against me as a worker. Workers still believe that.
The gold mining industry as had a bad reputation. However, over the last 15 or 20 years they have been closely supervised by the government. Because their books have been looked at by the government, because all emergency gold mining assistance was paid only after the mine showed the government its books, 1 am sure the situation which I knew 25 years ago has changed. I think that now those mines can be trusted, but I believe they are doubtful as to whether they can trust each other. The same is true of cobalt. They send their assays to a mill owned by the provincial government, and they send their ores there which are tested. The mining company which sends its ores there knows full well it will get exactly
Borrowing Authority
what they sent; there is no question about the honesty of that particular mill. But there have always been questions about some of the other custom mills.
However, in my opinion, the government cannot guarantee the price of gold. To do that, it would have to go back to the gold standard; it would have to establish the gold standard for Canada, and people are not yet ready for that. Most individuals in the world who are well off today have gone back to the gold standard. They have decided it is better to buy the Kruger Rand, the Maple Leaf coin or the old English guinea because governments back those coins so far as their quality and weight are concerned and they are better deals than the American dollar, treasury notes, mortgages, debentures, or other such things.
For that reason, the price of gold has risen to unreasonably high levels. I suggest that if this government enters into the mining industry and finds a way to start operating gold mines, it would be able to buy offshore oil without the price escalating one iota. Probably the total reason for the inflationary rise in our dollar is the escalation of the price of gold, and that is probably close to the inflationary factor in the world today. The government might find that they would get the same amount of oil for one ounce of gold today as they did ten years ago when the price of oil was considerably lower, and so was the price of gold. It might even be able to buy more oil than it did then. But it seems to me that we should not let those people in the Department of Finance who have studied under Keynes, who believe sincerely in the Bretton Woods Agreement and who were involved in the setting up of the International Monetary Fund, dominate our thinking on what you and I would like as a hedge against inflation. Rather than going out and borrowing $7 billion at 14 per cent tomorrow, we could use a small amount of that money for developing a gold mining industry in conjunction with the government so that we as Canadians could use that gold to make the lot of future generations in Canada much easier as a result of the elimination of much of our foreign debt.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, no more speeches. Having waited so long for the end of this debate, I will not speak for very long, but I think 1 have to reply to some of the points that were made.
Let me come back first to the principle of this bill to authorize the government to borrow $7 billion up to the end of this financial year. One of the features of this bill is that if $7 billion is not borrowed by the government by March 31, 1980, the borrowing authority will die and we will have to come back to the House to ask for further authority to borrow funds.
Why do we have to borrow $7 billion? We have to borrow that amount because the previous government-I know hon. members opposite do not like to hear the previous government mentioned, are ashamed to hear it mentioned-brought down a budget last year. In that budget there is a deficit. What is

the deficit? Well, the deficit in the budget brought in by the hon. member for Saint-Maurice (Mr. Chretien) last November 16 was $11,300 million.
If one spends $11,300 million more than one has, one has to get the $11,300 million from somewhere. Where does one get it from? One gets it from people who lend money. How does one get people to lend money? You ask the House to give the authority to borrow the necessary funds. Why are we not asking the House for authority to borrow $11,300 million? It is because we did not need the authority to borrow $11,300 million. Due to the authorities given by this House in previous years, it was tucked away here and tucked away there, in this pocket here or that little cubbyhole there. It was borrowing authority that had never been cancelled by the House. So we discovered that we only needed to borrow or to ask the House to give us authority to borrow $7 billion, because the government had previous authority from other sources to borrow the rest. So we are only asking the House to give us the authority to borrow what appears to be absolutely necessary, although we could have come in, as our Liberal predecessors did last year, and asked the House to authorize $10 billion.
It was hon. members opposite who are now members of the official opposition that asked this House in the income tax legislation earlier in 1979 to authorize them to borrow $10 billion. So we are coming in and asking the House for the authority to borrow $3 billion less than the official opposition requested when it was the government. Lo and behold, members of the official opposition are on their feet condemning us; it is a shocking thing we have done, to ask this House to let us borrow $7 billion. It is dastardly; it is absolutely astounding that we have the audacity to do this!
If we do not do it, where will we get the money to spend in accordance with the estimates that they prepared for the House? Are we going to manufacture it out of thin air?

Where are we going to get it? Do we ask members to surrender the gold from their teeth? I hear the hon. gentleman talking about gold mining. We had to ask the House to authorize this $7 billion borrowing, because we are carrying out the budget left to us by the hon. gentlemen opposite.
I was shocked and amazed. I will not describe it with an adjective because I want to get on with everybody in the House, particularly in view of the fact that they take so long when they are discussing a bill. I will not describe how unusual that behaviour is. We are talked at for four days because we asked for $7 billion to do the job that hon. gentlemen opposite wanted $10 billion authority to do. Certainly it is most peculiar. One would almost think that they are playing partisan politics.

Never, never.

They are chastising us because we asked for $7 billion of borrowing authority. They had the-what can one call it? They had the unmitigated gall-

Yes, that is putting it mildly. They had the unmitigated gall to say that we should not ask for this borrowing authority before the budget. They came here some 12 months ago to ask for some borrowing authority before they brought down a budget and before they presented any estimates to the House. The House had no estimates before it. We are asking for a borrowing authority. Not only is there a budget of last November, a year ago, but the estimates have been before the House since before the House was dissolved, if I remember correctly. So all the estimates are before the House, and the supplementary estimates.
Everyone knows how we plan to spend the money, there is no confusion about that.Yet it is suggested by hon. gentlemen opposite, such as the new finance critic-where was he when he was needed? Where was he when he should have been minister of finance? Where was he when he should have been putting his new views before the people of Canada? Where was he for the last four or five years? He was relegated to another role. Certainly he was not in cabinet, and now he is being trotted out. He is being trotted out because the hon. member for Saint-Maurice is afraid to get up in the House and ask a financial question. He dare not ask one, knowing how silly he will sound if he does. The hon. member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray) was the one who said that we should not get borrowing authority because we do not have a budget yet.
I suppose there is not much point in getting into the debate on interest rates at this stage, although a lot of members opposite raised it. We will have other occasions. As a matter of fact, 1 have been attacked in the House because it was alleged that I did not want to go before the House of Commons Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1979-80 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY FOR 1979-80

It was wrongly alleged that I did not want to go there until after Governor Bouey had been there. I did not want to go there until Governor Bouey had been there because Governor Bouey wanted to go before I was there. He wanted to do as had always been done in the past, to appear first and the minister would appear after. But I am more than willing to go. I am going to be there tomorrow morning.
We had a motion here today to allow the whole matter to be televised. These ferocious lions opposite have been attacking me because I will not go before the House of Commons finance committee, implying that I am afraid to answer their questions. We want the television cameras there so that the people of Canada can see what is being said and asked there.
October 29, 1979

We requested that and moved a motion today. The hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Clarke) moved the motion. The member who accused me in the House of refusing to go before the committee, a member from Montreal, the hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert), said no and would not allow the motion to be approved.
I am neither afraid to go before the committee nor afraid to go before the committee televised. But apparently the hon. gentlemen in the official opposition do not want that. They do not want the people of Canada to see the clarity of my answers, the way in which 1 handle their questions, and the way in which I will point out to them what they said a few months ago, a few weeks ago, a year ago, two years ago, and what the hon. member for Saint-Maurice said and did not say.
I could stand up in this House any day of the week and just copy the answers of the former minister of finance.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1979-80 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY FOR 1979-80
speechtext: You have done that.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1979-80 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY FOR 1979-80
speechtext:
No, 1 have not needed to do that. I have been able to dream up the same reasons myself! 1 say that I hope hon. gentlemen tomorrow will allow us to have television cameras in this committee.
One of the hon. ladies from Vancouver talked about the Titanic. 1 guess it is like the Titanic. We have a crew over here that is pumping her out. The Titanic was on her way down, if we want to compare the Canadian economy to the Titanic, and the captain and the crew over here are pumping her out as fast as we can. When we are able to bring in our fiscal policy to complement the monetary policy, then we will get Canada on the way again. We are not expecting that governor Bouey and his monetary policy can do this job. It cannot be done with monetary policy alone. It has to be done with a combination of monetary policy and fiscal policy.
Two great things which are so hurting the economy of this country and causing the huge budgetary deficit which we must start eliminating in a healthy manner are overspending and too much tax reduction, leading to a great deficit. That must be cut back if there is going to be a chance to get ahead with the huge deficit in the balance of payments in our international account. That has got to be dealt with. These things take time. What is the good of hon. gentlemen getting up in the House and saying that we should not pay interest, that we should not pay dividends to outside investors, that we should stop doing this? So what? If we stop doing this right now, if from tomorrow onward we pay no extra interest or no extra dividends to outside investors, we would still have to pay those who have already invested and lent us money. We would still have this problem. It would still be a problem for another two, three, four or five years. We were a long time getting to this position, and we are going to be a pretty long time getting out of it. It is not something anyone can cure overnight.
The hon. gentlemen from the NDP say that we should stop this, that we should stop foreign investment and that we should stop borrowing more money abroad. What are we supposed to do? Are we supposed to wave a magic wand so that we can suddenly stop paying out these billions of dollars which Cana-
B or rowing Authority
dians and governments in Canada owe to foreign investors and foreign lenders? We cannot do that. This is a problem that nobody has a magic wand to cure. Since 1945 this country has been allowing itself to become more and more economically dependent on the United States of America. It is not something that started on June 5 when we became the government; that is a situation which has been building up and building up for the last 30 or 40 years. Now 70 per cent of our exports go to the United States and 70 per cent of our imports come from the United States. We have a lot of our industry owned by the Americans and outside investors. We borrow huge sums outside Canada. So that is not something we can reverse overnight. That is not something we will reverse this year. That is not something that can be reversed this year and next year together. It will not be reversed the year after or the year after that either. It is something which we start with now, and if we are successful we may have a good chance at starting a reversal and bringing the current account deficit down over the next four or five years.
That is our message to the Canadian public. We cannot undo all this damage overnight, no one can. There is no magic wand. That is the course we will start on. Because if we do not start somewhere we will never get there. If one does not start on the road, one will never get to the end of it. 1 will not go into any more detail now, it is not the proper time. We will have lots of time to debate that matter in the coming budget debate.
I was chastised because I was a bit lighthearted when I debated the introduction of this bill. While debating in this House, I try to enjoy the debate, to poke some fun at the other side and so on. A number of sourpusses opposite got up and attacked me as though there was something unhealthy or wrong with trying to enjoy oneself when debating a measure in this House and trying to show one's sense of humour. God knows, 1 have little to laugh about. If 1 cannot get up and attempt a jest or two in this House, I will be in pretty bad shape. It will be pretty gloomy.
As the hon. gentleman from British Columbia pointed out the other day, I was not looking happy, and I explained the reason why. I went through this before, starting back in 1972. I did not smile for three years while 1 was minister of finance in Newfoundland. Now I am trying a different approach and I am being attacked in the House for taking this matter all too lightly. If the Canadian Minister of Finance must go around looking like the hunchback of Notre Dame, 1 will do it to avoid being attacked. You have seen my last smile or chuckle in this House, Mr. Speaker.
The hon. member for Saint-Maurice got up the other day and said there was nothing funny about this matter. He said that the situation was not funny. The hon. member should certainly know that the situation is not funny because he left me this unfunny situation. If 1 am to listen to his advice, 1 will have to be lugubrious. One must be very lugubrious if one is to

be Minister of Finance in this House. From now on "lugubriousness" is the order of the day.
What else is there? Did anybody else say anything of any note? The hon. member for Saint-Maurice said that the countries that have oil do not charge the full price for their oil. He gave the example of Venezuala. That may be true. I have not checked out Venezuela, but 1 know that the United Kingdom has lots of oil in their North Sea, and that if anybody visits the United Kingdom they will find out what they charge for oil and gasoline. The western industrialized countries that have their own indigenous supplies of oil are paying the full international price. That will come to us over the next three or four years, also under our carefully worked out policy, which will be expanded on in every detail once the final flourishing touches are put to it after the first ministers have met.
We will tackle the pricing of oil because it was never attacked by our predecessors. We know that until that problem is tackled and resolved there will not be any major improvement in our economic activity, it cannot be done until we have dealt fairly with Alberta and with this country and put before the people of Canada, and had accepted by them, a policy that will lead us in three to four years' time-always keeping in mind U.S. prices-to the full value of our oil and gas products. We are going to tackle that problem. We are not going to evade it. We do not want to do that, because the Canadian public do not want cosmetic improvements, they want action.
I want a budget, Mr. Speaker. I have been waiting since June 5 to have a chance to bring a budget into this House. 1 plead with hon. members opposite to help me in doing that by passing, for example, this legislation, after reasonable discussion and debate, and the bills remaining from the last budget of the previous minister of finance, so that we have the decks clear and can get on with discussing it.
If that can be done within a reasonable period of time, I am hoping to bring a budget into this House before the end of November. My budget will outline what we think the fiscal and monetary answers are to the problems of this country. I do not want people to think that the solutions will not cause some hurt. There is no painless way to overcome inflation or these other economic problems we face in Canada. We only hope that the process will be as short as possible. We will have a budget as soon as this honourable House permits us to have a budget and to get on with it.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) said he had no objection to deficit financing. That is a well known fact and I will not even comment on it. We know that the hon. members in the NDP have no objection to deficit financing. It is the only kind of financing they understand.
After having been criticized by hon. members opposite for not going to the House of Commons finance committee and after their having said how eager they were to have Governor Bouey and myself come to the committee, the other afternoon, in the middle of this debate, an hon. member moved that the debate adjourn. He interrupted Governor Bouey in his testimony before the finance committee, and interfered with all the
[Mr. Crosbie.)
questioners because we were brought back to the House. As a result, an hour to an hour and a halFs time was lost in questioning Governor Bouey. That shows that perhaps it was not strict impartiality with which they were approaching this matter.
The hon. member from Saskatchewan who is sometimes called "Nasty Nystrom" or "Nosy Nystrom"-1 have forgotten the name of his riding-said that I had had a conversion on the road to Damascus. Apparently 1 am allowed to move there. The hon. member said he did not want the government to borrow $7 billion and he accused me of being a right-winger. I say that the hon. member is a "left-footer". He wanted to know why we should need to borrow $7 billion.
1 would like to know what the NDP would like us to cut out of our budget to offset this $7 billion in spending. Should we cut out the social security cheques? Should we do away with the child tax credit? Should we do away with payments to veterans? Is that what the hon. gentlemen of that party want us to cut to make up the $7 billion? We are borrowing this money to carry out these programs. The hon. member did not say exactly why we do not need this $7 billion, and he would not tell me what to cut out of the expenditures.
The hon. member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Baker), who is not here today, talked about the arterial road water supply system in the riding of St. John's West. I plead guilty to giving my constituents good service. I can promise them that if they keep returning me to this chamber, as long as I have a breath left in my body I will certainly do the best I can for my constituents in St. John's West, just as the hon. member is doing for his constituents in the riding of Gander-Twillingate. But just because the hon. member is not doing as well as I am, there is no need for him to point a finger in scorn at me. The only advice that I can give to the people in his riding is that they get rid of a member who cannot get them as much as the member for St. John's West can, and try and do better. I have to admit that it took seven to eight years before those expenditures were made on this arterial road, the metropolitan water supply system and the like. I can also say to the member for Gander-Twillingate that if he needs a hand to find his way around the new government, give me a call. The hon. member is a good friend of mine, and I can remember when we were together in previous times. He ran for our party in the provincial election in 1971.

He ran for the Conservative party. It was after my conversion. The hon. member for Gander-Twillingate converted to the PC's, he reconverted to the Liberals and God knows where he is now. He is reconstituted somewhere. It would do the hon. gentlemen opposite some good to get converted. I suggest they come over here and see what it is like and get off that left foot.
1 think that I have pretty well touched on everything, Mr. Speaker. There was a lot of talk about loan sharks and the like but I will let that subject go until another time. The member for Sault Ste. Marie (Mr. Symes) asked "Who cares?" Obvi-
October 29, 1979

ously the one who cares is me. 1 am asking the House to provide the $7 billion because we care. Next year we hope to approach the House for less. That will be part of our approach to the economic problems of Canada.
The hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) said this afternoon that we are paying high interest rates because there was a mistake in the money supply figures in the United States of America. That is absolute, unadulterated twaddle. There was a mistake made in the United States in the money supply figures, but that does not mean that they would not have raised their interest rates in any event. The Citibank raised its interest rate to 15.25 per cent last Friday, just after that mistake had been discovered. If the Americans would drop their interest rates this week, we would be able to consider where we are and hopefully drop ours. But just because they made a mistake in adding up the total of their money supply several weeks ago, has nothing to do with what interest rates are here today in Canada.
Nobody in the opposition asked a question today about whether the seven economists quoted in The Globe and Mail on October 29 were correct when they said that Canada may be able to escape double digit inflation. We did not hear any questions like that. Nobody on the other side asked whether these economists were right when they warned against overemphasizing energy prices in considering inflation. When we listen to hon. gentlemen opposite we might think that if energy prices go up, the cost of living is going to go out of sight. These seven economists-and there will be a hundred more to join them-say we should not overemphasize the importance of energy prices in considering inflation. The Globe and Mail article reports these economists as giving the following warning:
-in the consumer price index itself, energy prices have a direct weight of only 6.2 per cent, equal to the weight assigned to sales of tobacco and alcohol.
Let us get this in prespective. Hon. members on the other side of the House should not get hysterical. Let us keep this in perspective. I refer particularly to those members who were once in the government. They were there for 16 years so they should have learned something. The article continues:
Various other items have a far greater importance, such as food (21.5 per cent), housing (34.1), clothing (10.1) and transportation (15.8).
The economists point out that when we talk about increases in energy prices we should keep it all in perspective and that other matters are far more important in causing the cost of living to go up.
Mr. Speaker, 76 per cent support our mortgage proposal. 1 did not make that up; that is the result of the Gallup poll. It is the mortgage and property tax credit plan that hon. gentlemen opposite have been scoffing at for the last three or four days, particularly the hon. member from Manitoba. As I say, 76 per cent support the mortgage proposal-76 per cent, Mr. Speaker. I hope hon. gentlemen are going to help us get it through the House, Mr. Speaker, so that we can have it all in effect by Christmas.
Borrowing Authority
The Bank of America predicts that Canada's economy will show moderate acceleration in 1980 after three years of more modest growth. They approve what we are doing in Canada. A report in the Toronto Star of October 19 refers to the Bank of America's opinion that this government has taken the following action:
-announced plans to encourage the development of a free-market economy and to reduce the role of the public sector.
This has resulted in spending cuts, a reduction of government transfers, and lower taxes, all of which bode well for the long-term prospects of the Canadian economy.
That is the view of the mighty Bank of America, Mr. Speaker. The bank also expressed the view that spending should accelerate in Canada next year, bolstered by continuing profit growth. The Bank of America has more faith in Canada than hon. gentlemen opposite. I could go on and on, Mr. Speaker, but I just have a small selection here. The October 26 edition of The Globe and Mail had an editorial in support of the attempts we are making to get this economy back on the track.
I have here an article by a rare bird, a Liberal, who gave his views frankly and honestly. I believe Mr. David Greenspan is a Liberal. He ran for them, so he must be a Liberal. I do not know whether he would run for them now. He is a Toronto lawyer and author of the report of the federal-provincial land prices study done for the government. He gives the mortgage tax credit plan full support, saying that a mortgage plan will help tenants acquire new homes and owners to carry existing houses. I would ask hon. gentlemen to read this, particularly those in the official opposition. This is their expert whom they appointed to head a royal commission, the federal provincial land prices study, and who supports this plan fully. In this article he wrote:
A mortgage relief scheme would help not only one large group of tenants to acquire new housing, but also homeowners to carry their homes. They are struggling with the triple whammy of high interest rates, high house prices and high mortgage amounts (made possible by low downpayment requirements).
He went on to deal with some of the objections that have been made to the scheme. He wrote:
Mortgage-relief schemes will continue to be attacked, by bureaucrats, economists and upper-middle-class trendies.
That is the group we have been hearing from across the House-the "upper middle class trendies" with their shot cuffs and whatnot, their lace cuffs. They are against this mortgage tax credit scheme of ours. When we come to that bill I will deal with this article more fully. I just want to point it out to hon. gentlemen now in the hope they will change and be more helpful at that time.
I think that is all I should say at this time, Mr. Speaker. 1 will note the points worth noting made by hon. gentlemen opposite. This will not take too long. Quite seriously, Mr. Speaker, 1 will try to keep my ears open to hear what they are suggesting that is worthy of an attempt to carry out. I shall be glad to have any advice from them privately any time they want to give it. I hope that by working together-we will not always agree-and with hearty debate, this House of Com-
