speechtext:
No, Mr. Speaker, this is strictly attending to business in my new morose, lugubrious style.
This is a piece of legislation, which 1 will be moving should have second reading and be referred to the Committee of the Whole House, over which I do not want to take too long but just give some of the main measures contained in the legislation. Essentially the bill contains the income tax measures of the last budget of our predecessor administration. It was introduced in the budget of November 16, 1978. After reviewing these measures last summer, I announced on July 26 that 1 would be reintroducing most of the tax measures proposed by our predecessor. This was a statement made to attempt to eliminate uncertainty for taxpayers who were already conducting their affairs on the basis of that budget.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, it is the practice, once a budget is brought down in the House, That most of the changes are instituted and go into effect from the night the budget is brought down. Of course, many of the measures in the November 16 budget were of that nature.
The major measures in this bill include the following: first, the 3 per cent employment expense deduction will be increased once the measure is passed from $250 to $500, commencing with the 1979 taxation year. That is an improvement for individual taxpayers.
Second, the income tax credit and research and development tax credit will be enriched and extended. The credits will be extended indefinitely beyond the present July 1, 1980 termination date. The present rates of the investment tax credit of 5 per cent, 7.5 per cent and 10 per cent will be increased to 7 per cent, 10 per cent and 20 per cent respectively. The highest rates of credit would apply in the Atlantic provinces and the Gaspe region of Quebec, the middle rates will apply in the rest of Quebec-excluding the Montreal-Hull corridor-northern Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, northern Alberta, northern British Columbia and the Yukon and Northwest Territories. The 7 per cent investment tax credit will be extended to transportation equipment. That is defined to include commer-

cial aircraft, railway and shipping assets, intercity buses and long haul trucks.
The basic tax credit of 5 per cent of current and capital expenditures on R and D will be raised to 10 per cent for most regions and to 20 per cent for the Atlantic provinces and the Gaspe region. The tax credit will be increased to 25 per cent for R and D expenditures by a Canadian controlled private corporation which qualifies for the low small business tax rates. So that is the investment tax credit in R and D.
The third major item is that the drilling fund incentive allowing a 100 per cent write-off for Canadian exploration expenses incurred by individuals and non-resource corporations will be extended to December 31, 1981.
The fourth measure is a very important item. Financial institutions-and that includes, Mr. Speaker, banks, life insurance companies and trust companies, among others-will become taxable on their earnings from term preferred shares and income debentures issued after November 16, 1978. That became a very serious problem, Mr. Speaker, and when we get into Committee of the Whole no doubt hon. members will want information on what use was made of those kinds of instruments in the months and years leading up to the budget of November 16. We will see that truly astounding amounts of financing were being done by the use of so-called after tax instruments, term preferred shares and income debentures. That had a very significant effect on the taxable income of banks and other companies that were using them. We are continuing with that provision which makes it impossible for this kind of financing to be used, except for its original purpose, after November 16 of last fall.
The bill also contains a number of other important measures. These include tax relief for the RRSP funds, passing on death to dependent children when there is no spouse-that is to assist dependent children; the ability to deduct immediately interest and property taxes on land awaiting development; to permit the deductibility of underwriting expenses; changes in the valuation of inventories to prevent a deduction for both depreciation and capital cost allowance; changes in the tax treatment of payments on termination of employment; and the taxation of income from deferred annuities.
One area where there is a fairly major change from what was originally contemplated in the legislation of the last administration has to do with the question of taxation of small business.
In addition to that change, which I will come to in a minute, there are a number of other changes of a technical nature which are to remove ambiguities or improve clarity. Most of them are as a result of representations made by taxpayers since the budget of last November, but some include measures themselves that were in the budget. For example, under this bill, interest-free housing loans may be made to both the husband and his spouse, and if the combined loans are within the existing $50,000 limit, there will not be a benefit for income tax purposes. In other words, you will not be taxed;
October 29, 1979

you will not be treated as though you had a benefit. Previously the loan could not be divided between husband and wife, but this bill will permit that.
Also, the measures regarding deferred life annuities will now have effect only for contracts entered into after November 16, 1978, rather than after the end of 1977.
As 1 indicated a few moments ago, and as I indicated in my press release of October 23, we have conducted a further review of the measures contained in the Liberal administration's bill relating to the small business deduction. Under the proposals introduced in the budget of the hon. member for Saint-Maurice (Mr. Chretien), aside from income from property, the benefits of the special corporate tax rate on small business would have been denied to three categories of business income. First, you could not get the benefit of the small business tax rate of 25 per cent under the last budget provisions if your company's income was from property in the form of interest, or interest just from property, not active business. That is one area that was affected. Under the proposed legislation companies not permitted to get the small business tax rate of 25 per cent went back up to the normal tax rate of anywhere between 46 per cent and 50 per cent.
In addition to companies that receive their income simply from ownership or leasing of property, the benefits of the special corporate tax rate on small business would have been denied to three categories; that is to say, professional income of lawyers, doctors, chartered accountants, income from certain personal services as well as income from the provision of certain management and other administrative services. For a small business that came within one of these defined categories, the tax rate was changed from 25 per cent to the tax rate that applies to corporations generally, which would range in amount, I think, from 46 per cent to 51 per cent, depending upon the province in which you are situated.
As hon. ladies and gentlemen of the House will know, the small business deduction is available for Canadian-controlled private corporations that carry on an active business. They get a rate of 25 per cent. For a manufacturing or processing business it is 20 per cent. Those reduced rates apply to $150,000 of eligible income annually until the corporation's accumulated income exceeds $750,000. Income in excess of that amount is taxed at the full rate.
The reason for making a change in this area in the first place I will try to explain now. The small business deduction represents forgone federal tax revenue of about $1 billion annually. It costs the Government of Canada approximately $1 billion annually to give the small business tax rate. Our existing tax system recognizes a partial or total integration of corporate and personal taxes. That is achieved through the dividend tax credit. Under that, a shareholder is required to gross-up any dividend he receives, and he is allowed a tax credit in the amount of the gross-up. Until 1977 the dividend gross-up was 33W per cent. There was full integration between personal and corporate income achieved for corporate income which had been subject to the corporate tax of 25 per cent. If
Income Tax Act
the corporate tax exceeded 25 per cent, then there is only partial integration; there was some double taxation.
In 1977 the dividend tax credit was increased from 33'/3 per cent to 50 per cent. The result of that was that the tax credit on dividends exceeds the amount of corporate tax paid, wherever the corporate tax is less than 331/3 per cent. In other words, there was overintegration in that kind of situation. After 1977 when the dividend tax credit was increased to 50 per cent, if there was a situation where the corporation paid a tax rate of less than 33W per cent, there was overintegration compared to the personal tax system. So it was much to the benefit of a person to incorporate for his personal services if he could do so. By doing this he would save taxes, and in addition he would have a tax deferral.
This was a device that came to be much used by the categories of people I have mentioned, and by people just getting income from property. It did not fit into the original reason for giving the small business tax rate, which was to encourage entrepreneurs, risk-takers and small business to go into processing and manufacturing and the service industries where more risks had to be taken than the usual professional takes. I will not go into all the reasons at this stage.
There came to be two significant tax attractions in trying to incorporate. One, there was a tax deferral as long as the income was left in the corporation. Second, even when the income was distributed through a dividend, you were still getting a tax benefit.
The method chosen by the Liberal administration to try to correct this with certain groups of people was to target them, and to say that they would have to pay the full corporation tax rate, not the 25 per cent rate. There were a lot of people very much upset by that. This applied specifically to incorporated employees, namely taxpayers who usually provide services in master-servant relationships. They might be executives, athletes or salesmen on commission. These were people incorporating and using the lower rate although the real form of their activity had not changed. There were incorporated professions, such as doctors, lawyers and other professions who could incorporate and did so wherever the provincial laws or professional ethics allowed them to do so and get the lower rate. There were a lot of incorporated service companies, corporations in most cases, established by the wife of a professional who would provide management and administrative services to his particular profession and siphon off the professional income which would then qualify for the lower tax rate.
There were a tremendous number of objections to the proposals made by the last administration and there were a great many representations made to me by members of our government caucus to take a different approach. Members of the caucus wanted this loophole plugged, but wanted it done in a more fair and equitable manner for the people involved.
There were also several alternatives which the Liberal administration could have chosen. There were three ways of approaching this problem. We have chosen a different alternative. With regard to these categories of business activity, we are going to establish a third tax rate to apply to the incorpo-

October 29, 1979
Income Tax Act
rated employee, the incorporated professions and the incorporated service company. The tax rate will be 33'A per cent. They will not be put back in the tax bracket of anywhere from 46 to 50 per cent. They will not have the advantage of the 25 per cent small business tax rate. They will have a new rate of 3395 per cent as a recognition of their special position.
The result will be this. Because the corporation will pay 33'A per cent when they pay their dividends out, and the dividend tax credit was in effect since 1977, the amount of tax for which they are receiving credit will approximate the amount of tax paid by the corporation. Therefore, there is no immediate tax advantage to paying dividends to themselves in that way. In addition, those new rules are going to be in the statute and not in the regulations.
There is still an advantage to persons in this category, because as long as they leave the income that the corporation is making in the corporation, they will be deferring tax. It will only be subject to the 33 A per cent new small business rate. As long as they are income tax payers who earn a taxable income in excess of $15,000, they will get a tax advantage by leaving the income in the corporation. In other words, if the person who has such a corporation is a taxpayer earning in excess of $15,000 in taxable income a year, it is an advantage to him to leave the income in the corporation for the purpose of the corporation rather than take it out. There is still an advantage in tax deferral for such a person.
This is the method we are suggesting to solve the problem of the small business tax rate. The changed provisions will be found in the legislation before us. These changes would apply to taxation years that commence after 1979 for corporations that were in existence on October 23, 1979, and to all taxation years for corporations formed after that date.
All Canadian business income other than investment income in those three categories of corporations affected by this change will be subject to a 33A per cent small business tax rate and also given time to rearrange their affairs so they can receive the benefit of this small business tax rate on eligible active business income. Some of them may not be able to arrange their affairs before the end of the year. When that is the case, the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Baker) has indicated he is prepared to allow them to reorganize in light of these amendments so that they can change their fiscal year end in 1980.
There are a lot of other provisions in these income tax amendments before hon. members. After second reading and when this bill goes to Committee of the Whole, we will deal with it clause by clause. I do not want to be too long today. I want to conclude by saying that the one major change we have made to this legislation is a definite improvement. We hope hon. members opposite will agree with us.
The proposed legislation has had a very long delay. It was introduced in the budget almost a year ago. This has created a lot of confusion and uncertainty in the minds of taxpayers. It is to be regretted that these measures were not put before

Parliament and given priority to ensure their passage before the House dissolved last March.
I wish to remind the House that taxpayers who filled 1978 returns on the basis of measures in this bill have not yet had their returns processed. There are thousands of taxpayers who filled their 1978 returns based on the changes contained in this bill. The Department of National Revenue cannot process these returns until this bill is passed, until they know whether this House is going to make the changes announced a year ago and pass them into law. For that reason, it would be well for us to pass this bill as soon as reasonably possible. I believe the taxpayers certainly have had their patience pushed to the limit in having to wait this long. Hopefully it will not happen again. I remind hon. members that it is necessary for us to try and clear this out of the way before a new budget.
I hope we can count on the support of members in the official opposition whose legislation in large part this is, with the exception of one major change that I have outlined and which I hope they will also be able to support. I also hope that my confreres in the New Democratic Party will see fit to do this as well. If they have any objections, they should make these known and make their points; but I hope they will let this bill through in a reasonable period of time so that we can get on with the next budget.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill obviously is to pass into formal law the proposals in the budget of November, 1978 presented by the last Liberal government. It is not necessary for me to outline the measures in that budget because the Minister of Finance (Mr. Crosbie) has done so. He has done so with approval. He has put forward with approval all the measures in the last budget, except perhaps one which he has changed somewhat. However, basically he has retained the essential objective of that measure as well.
As the minister pointed out, the measures in this budget as a practical matter have been in effect since the date of the budget even though the legislation had not been passed at the time the House was dissolved for the last election. As we know, generally budget measures are considered to be in effect from the time the budget speech is read, unless the speech specifies otherwise. The idea behind this is that a government is supposed to command enough support in Parliament to ensure the budget proposals are passed into law, even though the legislation for that purpose is not passed until some months after the date of the budget speech. However, a change in government creates some uncertainty. That is an understatement when it comes to this new Conservative government. In any case, uncertainty was created as to whether this new government would proceed with the measures in the last budget.
The Minister of Finance stated at his press conference last July that he would remove this uncertainty. He announced at that time that the new Conservative government intended to enact into law almost without change the measures proposed in the last Liberal budget. It is now almost half a year after this new Conservative government took office. The Minister of Finance, as his initial solution to the problems and needs of
October 29, 1979

this country, is asking this House to enact into law the budget of the previous Liberal government.
What better confirmation could there be of the value of these measures? What better endorsement could there be of these measures than the actions today of this new Conservative government? What a contrast with the scorn heaped on these measures during the budget debate last November by the hon. member for York-Simcoe, now the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Stevens), when he was official spokesman on financial matters in the official opposition. He concluded his speech by saying: "In short, in great contrast to the budget last night, we would bring in a budget, given the opportunity, which would restore for Canadians the visions they see for Canada." Here they have done so by presenting to this House with approval and endorsement the budget of the preceding Liberal government.
In allowing the budget measures of the previous Liberal government, and in fact allowing Liberal economic policies generally, to continue in place for the five months since they took office is, as I have said, a confirmation and endorsement of those measures. This is not a case where a new government has taken office at the end or almost at the end of a fiscal year and where a budget statement had been made prior to that year's beginning with measures taking effect immediately on the date of the presentation of that speech. If that had been the case, the government would have had no practical alternative but to ask Parliament to pass into law the budgetary measures which had been in effect, to all intents and purposes, for that whole preceding period. But that is not the case here. The new Conservative government took office after only about two months had elapsed in the current fiscal year. It has had the opportunity and the authority to change the framework set by the last budget had it wished to do so. Instead, the budget has been allowed to remain unchanged for almost half a year.
This is one confirmation that at the time the government changed Canada's economy was in better shape than it had been for some time due to the kinds of policies to be found in the budget presented to us today by the Minister of Finance with a request for its speedy approval. That this was the situation and that it continued for several months after the election has been confirmed as well by the cost of living figures which were trending lower at the time the government changed than for some time previously. The unemployment rate was also trending lower at that time than had been the case.
Letting the budget continue virtually unchanged for almost half a year also shows that, contrary to what the Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) is saying, there was no new information of substance which would justify statements that the incoming administration had found the economy to be in worse shape than had been expected before taking office and as a result of which it was not possible for them to carry out their pledge to reduce interest rates, or to implement other promises of
Income Tax Act
immediate action with respect to the economy, made during or immediately before the election campaign.
Had there really been such evidence it would have been the obligation of the new government to call Parliament together immediately after the election and to put forward measures to deal with the serious situation they would have claimed to have found. After all, Margaret Thatcher and the British Conservatives were able to call the U.K. parliament into action only one week after their election; she was able to present a budget to that new parliament only four weeks after it had begun its sitting. But this did not happen when the new Conservative government came to power here. It did not take this step. Obviously this showed that not only was the economy in better shape than the Conservatives had claimed, but that they had no real idea what to do once elected to office.
Let us bear in mind, Mr. Speaker, that there have been some important changes in the economic situation since the presentation of the last budget in November, 1978. There has been the substantial OPEC oil price increase, confirmation of an economic downturn in the United States, and the beginnings of a serious economic downturn in our own country. This means important changes in the assumptions on which the previous budget was based. It means there is a need for the new government not simply to implement the budget which had not been passed at the time of the last election, but also to add to the useful basis it provided for the economy by presenting a new budget. So far it was failed to do so. A new budget has been needed to take into account the changed circumstances 1 have mentioned.
The new Conservative government may feel it does not have a lot of room to manoeuvre, but it certainly had some room. There is room for specific measures to help our economy become more productive and efficient, for example. In spite of the inactivity of the past five months and the appearance of inability to act that the new government has given, there was no need for it to be immobilized.
We should remember that it takes six months for budget measures to work their way through the economy. By the time the Conservatives get around to presenting their budget and by the time any useful measures in it take effect, it may be too late for them to have any beneficial effect, bearing in mind the harm the inaction and neglect of members opposite has already begun to do to Canada.
The new Conservative government has wasted the past five months. All they have done is allow interest rates to be raised to record levels even though, before the election, they said they would bring interest rates down. When he was leader of the opposition before the election, the Prime Minister did not say that a Conservative government would lower interest rates only after allowing them first of all to go to record levels. He did not say it would lower interest rates only if it found the economy to be in a certain position. That pledge was made without qualification or equivocation. The Conservatives now say they have information showing the state of the economy to be worse than they had thought, but they have been unable to present such information even though they were urged to do so

October 29, 1979
Income Tax Act
during today's question period. If there is such information, I challenge them to present it. But they cannot do so.
In fact, the Minister of Finance has undermined and contradicted the Prime Minister on this essential excuse they offer for their inactivity and for failing to carry out election promises on key issues, such as the lowering of interest rates. For instance, last Friday he made a special point of telling us how a leading economist, John Grant, had been quoted as stating that the Canadian economy was the strongest in the world. And today he took great pleasure in telling us that the Bank of America was saying nice things about the good state of the Canadian economy. Where does this leave the Prime Minister and his argument that there is some horrendous information about the shape of the Canadian economy which is in the possession of the government and which prevents them carrying out their election promises?
The Minister of Finance proved to us on Friday and again today, by his own words and the authorities he was citing, that that is just a lot of nonsense. All that the inactivity which has followed the election proves is that the Conservatives did not know what they were talking about before and during the election. It shows they did not have a clear idea of Canada's needs and what to do about them. They still do not and they have failed to show they have any capacity to carry out their responsibilities and serve the needs and interests of the people of Canada.
The Prime Minister admitted this today during question period. He explained why the government has done nothing at all in five months. He said he and his ministers needed some on-the-job training. What is wrong with that, he asked. I say there is plenty wrong with that. Before and during the election he said, in effect, that he had an experienced team of people ready and willing to take over the government of Canada immediately after the election and to give it new direction without delay. Instead, when his party was called upon to form the government nothing happened for five months except for the raising of interest rates and the spending of a period of on-the-job training for himself and his ministers at the expense of the Canadian taxpayers and the Canadian economy. Because of the need for this on-the-job training, the Conservative government has wasted the last five months. This is also shown by the emptiness of the Speech from the Throne with regard to such matters as the economy and energy.
The Minister of Finance cannot present a budget because he does not know what the price of energy is to be. Yet the government which pledged itself to institute a new atmosphere of federal-provincial co-operation is just standing back and letting its Conservative friends in Ontario and Alberta squabble among themselves, to the detriment of the whole of this country.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED TAX PAYMENT TO OFFSET WITHDRAWAL OF GOVERNMENT SERVICES
speechtext:
That when the government sells an asset such as a radar station or other public complex, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of requiring the department concerned to pay at least one additional year of property tax to a small municipality in order to help offset the sudden economic demands that are placed on the community which arise out of this transfer, sale arrangements and maintenance related thereto.
He said: Mr. Speaker, from time to time federal and provincial government facilities are built in very small municipalities. Sometimes these are built in sparsely populated areas for very good reasons, but they have a tremendous effect on those small communities. If one of them were to close down in a large city or major populated area, the effect would not be very great because there would always be something to take its place. However, when a military base, prison complex, radar station or any other agency of government of any size which is located in a small rural township, village or small town, closes down, there certainly are bad social and economic consequences.
First, the government moves in and purchases land. Preparation of the land for construction takes place after the design work has been done, and immediately the lifestyle of the local community starts to change because of construction jobs. Great hopes are raised for the future. New people come into
October 29, 1979

the municipality and mix with the old. This changes lifestyles with regard to education, skills and trades, and it affects every facet of everyday life, right down to the grocery store in the local village or town.
The government puts in new community services. It puts in, for example, water lines, sewer lines, sewage disposal plants, storm drains, filtration plants, schools, recreational facilities, housing and the major project for which the facility is meant. This alone creates a boom in the area. The nature of the land is very important, whether it be rock, sand or soil. The adjustment later on from a government institution or facility to a municipal institution or facility may be even more difficult because of the nature of the services. Today, with greater requirements imposed by departments of environment on sewage disposal, for example, it makes a great deal of difference whether the location is in the Canadian Shield, on good, solid clay ground or, indeed, on sand.
The federal government carries the financial load for keeping up all services and administration-budgeted through the Parliament of Canada-with all its financial and human resources, and those human resources also include expertise in various trades, right down to engineering services for the operation of the total complex. These are not the kinds of services small municipalities have at their disposal, nor indeed can they afford them.
Everything goes along well for a number of years, but if there is a situation in which the facility becomes outdated because it is no longer required or for some other reason, rumours start floating around that the total facility is going to close down, and a state of depression sets in on the over-all community and surrounding communities.
Elected people and other community leaders lobby to keep the facility open a little longer. They may gain one, two or three years' extension, but eventually the crunch comes. The government announcement about closure by a certain date brings about a series of events leading to a final disposal of the total site. First of all, if any federal department can use the establishment and wants it, then it does not go up for sale but simply begins the neat and tidy transfer from one department to another, with big government still footing the bills. If no federal department wants it, it is offered to the province for any of its departments which might be interested. Third, if no department of the provincial government wants it, then it is offered for sale to the municipality or to a group of municipalities such as those represented by a county council, in the case of Ontario. It is in the best interests of the local government, whether it is going to buy it or not, to put forward some ideas as to how it wants the facility used afterwards.
If the local government wants the facility to stay intact, it should request this, and this should go into the agreement with whoever buys the facility thereafter. There may be a real problem if it is not stated clearly how the transfer should be handled or what is wanted for the future of the facility in the municipality. I suppose we could say we are talking about a community here in the sense that the facility is really superimposed on the community by a senior level of government.
Municipal Taxes
It is important to have the desires of the community written into the agreement of sale. That is a must. If provincial or municipal governments do not want the facility, it then goes up for sale to the highest valid bidder who is willing to follow the guidelines laid down and who can meet the financial commitment of the down payment or deposit with the bid. The bidder must also demonstrate that he is financially capable of paying for the site in the long run.
From this point on the over-all community feels that it has a new lease on life, but in fact what has happened is that it is going through another major change in human environment. Adjustments will be necessary because the municipality is going from big government-supported facilities to dealing with an entirely different organization, and the facility is used for entirely different purposes.
We are beginning to realize how easy it was for a senior level of government to maintain and operate this new section of the community that is suddenly superimposed on the local municipality. Subdivision plans have to be drawn up, but a municipality may not want to take over the subdivision because they may not be able to afford to take over the services of the community, such as the water lines, sewers, filtration and sewer plants, and so on. All of us who are familiar with municipal politics are certainly aware of the cost of these facilities today. You might have a small municipality refusing to accept this responsibility, and certainly they cannot be blamed for that. Other ratepayers may accuse them of being irresponsible if they took that responsibility without having the wherewithal to pay for it. Furthermore, if the new owners do not live up to the agreements with the municipality and with other people, then the municipality is left holding the liability. The whole procedure can end up in messy lawsuits and in a feeling of instability and frustration.
I have discussed this matter at some length with many people at both levels of government. I find that no one has come to grips with the problem, but I think that as time goes on it will be more and more important that we do so. My recommendation in this motion today is that the municipality concerned should receive a grant in lieu of taxes at least equal to one year's taxes.
Second, there is a need for some instrument or instruments to take over to ease the burden on the municipality and help them on the road to a stable community and to become established by way of long-term rather than short-term solutions. The federal and provincial governments should provide personnel with expertise to advise and assist the municipality through the difficult period of change, because the smaller communities are not equipped, as 1 said before, with this type of professional and technical experience. Public instruments should come into play immediately whereby federal and provincial governments can come to an agreement of a type that will require the province, with federal assistance, to provide the expensive services for a period of, say, three to five years or until such time as an adjustment is made and the new commu-

October 29, 1979
Municipal Taxes
nity has evolved out of the old. With plans such as these, to thrust large institutions into the lap of small communities is simply like trying to float the Queen Mary in the Madawaska River, because small communities are in no way capable of raising that kind of money or setting up that kind of institution.
Another problem is that the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation, as it is now called, and provincial governments do not give grants to communities where the water and sewage services are already established. There are only programs through CMHC and the provincial governments for such facilities to be started, and this creates a real block. If the development of a community is rapid, then you do not run into the same problems, but it is not rapid in sparsely populated areas.
1 raise this issue because 1 feel that senior levels of government must come to grips with this serious situation that is created, and when they build an institution they do in fact create the problem in the beginning. They bring in all kinds of infrastructure, and then end up walking away from it and leaving all kinds of problems or repercussions behind. There are relatively few such cases but they do occur from time to time. It would not cost the two senior levels of government very much over a period of readjustment because, in checking the property sections of the Department of Public Works and Crown Assets, 1 learned that there are not many cases, but they do come up from time, and when they do they are serious.
1 hope that my main motion and my other suggestions will meet with the approval of members of the House. I know that when we put forward motions in the House, it is not common practice for a private member's motion to be adopted; but I want to say to my colleagues on both sides of the House that I air this problem because I think it is one that could be common to all of us in all parts of Canada. It is very important, if we are going to think nationally in this Parliament, that we get away from the idea of dumping things on small communities and walking away. It is not fair for any federal government, I do not care what party label it might carry, to do this, and I think this is a matter which could well be discussed at some federal-provincial meeting. It would not take a great deal of discussion, it would not take a great deal of money, and it is a solution which would take a great deal of pain out of municipal politics and in sparsely populated regions of Canada. I thank you, Mr. Speaker, and I thank members of the House for their attention.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to express my appreciation for the very reasoned argument that the hon. member for Renfrew-Nipissing-Pembroke (Mr. Hopkins) has presented to this House. I appreciate his concern because I have also spent some time in municipal government and appreciate the problems that actions of senior government can create for municipalities.
However, 1 should like to respond to the hon. member's motion at two different levels. First, I wish to address specifically the essence of the motion he has presented to the House

and, second, to address in a more general sense the more serious implication which the motion raises within my mind.
First, the motion implies that a municipality will suffer if the federal government sells real property within the municipality. I would say that that is not necessarily so. In fact, the opposite would be the case. The resolution gives no examples of the kind of "sudden economic demands" which would be placed on the community. But from the tax standpoint, it is hard to see where there would be a problem.
First, we should bear in mind that when the government sells real property, normally it becomes taxable as of the date of sale. The new owner becomes a regular taxpayer, and the municipality does not lose any tax revenue. Indeed, local government could well gain if the property is being sold to be transformed into some new commercial or industrial activity. We should bear in mind that federal grants in lieu of municipal taxes do not extend to cover business occupancy taxes levied by the municipality when the building is used by business. The new owner could well be adding to the building occupancy revenues of the local government when it is taken over by a private industrial concern.
We should not assume, as I think this resolution does, that the sale of government property inevitably creates economic demands on the local government. Indeed, the situation could be quite the reverse if the new buyer used the property for productive purposes. So, on this score, the resolution does not place much confidence in the ability of private enterprise or the private sector to generate new economic activity in Canada.
It is possible that in a particular situation the sale of some federal government property might create some demand on local government. But that does not mean we should assume such expenses will arise in every case and therefore we should provide a quite arbitrary cash transfer to local government of an additional year's federal payments in lieu of real estate taxes.
The resolution does not mention what could be an even greater problem for the municipality. That is the case where the government does not sell the property but rather closes down the activity being carried on previous to the government having to change the status of the property. Such things inevitably happen from time to time, but I do not think any hon. member of the House would try to argue in principle that particular activities of the federal government should never be closed down but should go on forever. When this happens in some municipality-that is, the closing of a federal enterprise or institution-surely it is preferable to try to sell the property for private business activity rather than simply close up the federal installation and see the federal employees move away from the community.
We cannot consider this issue in isolation without taking account of over-all financial relationships among different levels of government. In fact, this resolution argues for a special kind of federal aid to municipalities, something which
October 29, 1979

no other local taxpayer is required to do. If aid is required, why should it be provided through a program of grants in lieu of taxes? This is not a relief program. It has a completely different purpose. The real purpose of the program is to pay grants to municipalities equal to the real property taxes that would be payable if federal property were taxable property. If a private property owner sells property, his liability for taxes stops as of the date of the sale. Therefore he pays taxes up to that date only. Why should the federal government be different? Therein lies the point of my concern.
The attitude of some members opposite is implied in this motion, that there is a basic difference between whether the federal government or any government owns a piece of property or whether it is privately owned. No one would seriously suggest that if a private company owned a piece of property, and if circumstances were such that it had to close that property up, there should be some kind of a law or provision where it would have to pay to the municipality taxes beyond the date of the transfer or sale. Yet that is what is implied in this motion, that there is a basic difference between the federal government and private enterprise, and that the federal government should be expected to do that which we would never expect a private company to do.
It is the provinces, not the federal government, which have created the financial situation municipalities find themselves in today. They have limited the taxing powers of local governments almost entirely to property taxes. They have used the broader range of provincial taxes to finance transfer payments to local governments. Indeed, a whole range of municipal activities is closely circumscribed by provincial laws and regulations. Therefore, if some special financial aid is required by municipalities, should it not be more a concern for provincial governments? This is particularly so when one considers the size of the federal deficit against the relatively strong position of Canada's provincial treasuries.
This is the second over-all point of my concern. This is the aspect of the motion which disturbs me most. On reading between the lines 1 see that somewhere or other there is a public trough, and if we can only get some money from the federal treasury, it does not really count; it is not really money in the normal sense. When 1 hear some of the proposals of members opposite during emergency debates and question period, sometimes I become astounded. It would be very interesting to Canadian taxpayers if every time an hon. member proposed an expenditure of an additional sum of money to the Government of Canada, somewhere over the head of that hon. member there was a little calculator, and the calculator would shine in neon lights the cost of that provision across the country.

speechtext:
As a nation we are confronted with three real choices when it comes to government spending; A drastic reduction in expenditures, including cuts in programs which none of us really wants to see; a major increase in revenues, largely through increased taxation; and finally, national bankruptcy. The mindless spending of the previous administration had the effect of fueling inflation, debasing our currency and robbing our citizens of their savings. It is the difficult task of this administration, the new government, to restore common sense to government spending notwithstanding the opportunistic posturing of some members opposite. Certainly this motion does nothing to alleviate the very serious problems of fiscal balance and responsibility.
Already the federal government has major responsibilities where property sales lead to unemployment. Of course, these relate to unemployment insurance, the cost of retraining unemployed people and finding new jobs for them. Every time an enterprise in a community must close down, whatever the reason, we expect the federal government to be a party to moving in, to providing unemployment insurance to those who are displaced, to working with manpower counsellors on necessary retraining programs, to finding new jobs for those who have been dislocated from their former employment. The federal government has a very major role to play. It discharges that major role, in terms of enterprises which must close down, without assuming the cost of enterprises from which they will have no additional revenues, but from which there will be a net debt for Canadians.
Nothing that 1 h ,ve said should in any way be meant to denigrate the importance of municipal government. Local government bears a major share of the responsibility for shaping the environment in which people live. It provides many vital public services, including elementary and secondary edu-
____________________COMMONS DEBATES_______________ October 29, 1979
Municipal Taxes
cation, environmental protection, local transportation, police and fire protection and recreational services.
As a former municipal councillor, 1 appreciate the great pressure under which municipal governments find themselves today. Their costs are all greatly affected by inflation because municipal services, such as those used to employ teachers, civic workers, road builders and repairers, policemen and firemen, are largely labour-intensive acitivities. Largely these costs are in the form of increased salaries and wages. The only way municipalities in Canada can raise these funds, other than through transfer payments, is through taxes on real property. Perhaps this is a real gripe of the municipalities of Canada.
While the senior governments, the federal government and provincial governments, are obvious benefactors of the inflationary process in that their revenues tend to increase with inflation or even in excess of inflation, municipalities are different. Municipalities levy their rates in absolute dollars having regard for the assessment of property. The only way that municipalities can increase their revenue is to increase the mill rate, and the taxpayers then receive a notice indicating precisely how much more they will be paying for their municipal services than they paid the year before. This procedure puts real pressure on the municipalities, and they recognize that fact.
We know that the municipalities are looking to the senior governments and that there is a difficult situation. But I believe that there is no way implied in this motion that this problem can be redressed. It is neither logical, practical, equitable, or administratively sound, and it is based on the notion that the federal government is basically the public trough. That may have been the philosophy of the previous government, but it is not the philosophy of this government.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have just heard two different points of view, and I can see why they are different. The previous speaker comes from Mississauga, one of the fastest growing areas in the country. If a government facility such as Malton were to close down, that community would be able to put houses on the tarmac within a matter of two or three months. On the other hand the problems in northern Ontario, although Renfrew is not in northern Ontario, are different.
I know of the problems at Freemont where they have a little radar base, and I am aware that Landry Crossing was closed. Perhaps it has not closed entirely, but it has certainly slowed down. There were not more than seven dozen people in the area affected by the radar installation, but in areas where it was much more advisable for people to work for the government than it was to continue farming, the residents will certainly suffer. They probably cannot go back to farming, but there is nothing else. I know that this has happened in my region in the Ramorc area and at Lowther, just west of Kapuskasing. It has happened in a number of areas.
[Mr. Jupp.J
Lowther was particularly important because the United States were in there as well as the Canadian service. As a result more money was brought into the area. Many of these small communities made a sacrifice in rising to the occasion. In many cases the communities purchased firetrucks which they could not afford. They had to put in a water system. In the case of Matheson, in order to accommodate the base at Ramore, it put in a number of trailer sites complete with pads, septic tanks, and a water system. As soon as the base closed, it was no longer of any value and now has become a liability. The lots cannot be sold, they are not usable, and they are probably still under debenture.
These communities made great efforts to meet the requirements of the government and they did it at great expense. The radar base mentioned by the hon. member was very small. Very few people were involved, but those who where made an immense effort to ensure that it was successful and that it worked. The government has a responsibility to these people. They cannot say, "we do not need it, we are closing it; goodbye".
When these bases were abandoned the municipalities were not interested in purchasing what was left behind. As a result, most of what was left behind was sold privately, or dismantled and taken away. The communities could not afford to buy anything because they did not have any money, and instead of creating a tax base the items left behind became a liability. For example, 1 recently viewed the airport at Ramore, which had been put in by the Americans while they were there. It had grown in and there were trees growing four and Five feet high. The municipality had to go in and spend $1,000 to cut down the trees in the hope that some day the airport would again be useful and necessary to the area. There is also a building there which they have to protect. The municipality does not want to see this facility destroyed because they have hopes that something will replace the industry which has just left.
1 have heard that the government intends to close the facility at Landry Crossing. I have noticed lights there when I drive by, so presumably it is not closed. The facility is a minimum security penitentiary set out in the area of Petawawa army base. I am sure that the people located around that area have had to make some concessions in order to attract the facility to their area, but when it disappears they will be asked to take it over and do something with it, otherwise the government will suffer a total loss. Communities such as Landry Crossing do not have a ready use for such facilities. In many cases the facilities have been torn down and taken away, leaving a vacuum in the area. As a result, many of the services offered by the community are a total loss, but they are left with paying the debenture.
The hon. member is simply asking in his motion that we cushion the withdrawal for a period of one year by paying the property tax. He mentioned in his speech that perhaps five years for withdrawal on a graduated basis would be better. The five-year term on a graduated basis is probably the better idea because the communities will need less as time goes on.
October 29, 1979

In many case these communities were asked to make contributions and to participate as municipalities in the government development. They did not want the government to build a fence around the facility because then nobody would associate with the facility, and as a result they were sucked into setting up such things as recreational facilities and the like. One facility which almost all communities provided was firefighting equipment. Now with the government gone they can no longer afford it. In many cases we are talking about a community with approximately 20 families, and in some cases less, but they were stuck with being big sister to a relatively larger facility having probably more employees than the community had citizens.
Now the government has gone. My hon. friend, the member for Mississauga North (Mr. Jupp), has said, "let them go. We are not giving them welfare". In the first place it was the government that wanted the bases, and if the communities had been hostile it would have had a heck of a time moving into those areas. The people of these communities could have made it very difficult. The reason the bases were chosen was because it was best that the bases be located in areas where the radar would be most efficient. Now the government is saying, "Don't worry about them; they do not need handouts, it is not the Conservative way". I suggest that the hon. member will find, after he has been here for a while, that there are other things besides philosophy. There are such things as geography, and what is good for Mississauga is not necessarily good for Sioux Lookout, Lowther and Freemont. The situation is not the same.
It would not be satisfactory in Toronto. I remember many years ago, when you went up Yonge Street and north of Toronto on a streetcar, by the time you got to where Highway 401 is now, you were picking up milk cans and chickens, and after that you went on to Thornhill and Aurora. Now it is very hard to find those communities at all-they are downtown, and every time you go there are another ten buildings. I suppose the hon. member does not have to worry about it. He has enough trouble keeping the water system and the sewers and the streets growing fast enough to keep up with the population.
That is not the problem in most communities in northern Ontario, Mr. Speaker. We are just trying to service the ones we were asked to build as a favour to somebody else. We were anticipating, as we always do, the ultimate-that they were going to be there forever and we thought we could probably help them out by providing these facilities. We are not asking very much in this motion when we ask that those areas that have been asked to make that kind of contribution now receive a contribution that would be very valuable to the wind-down of those communities.
In your own case, Mr. Speaker, you may represent an urban area where you would find this to be a Mickey Mouse concession. You would find it to be undesirable and regressive. In fact, it would tie up property for one or two years and you
Municipal Taxes
could not get the high taxes out of it that you now do, so you would have to find a substitute for what may have been a long-term contract with the federal government, producing a limited revenue. This could be the situation in northern Ontario, in many cases.
If this motion is accepted the cost will not be very much, but it will certainly benefit those very, very small communities that have made a contribution, as Canadians, to the defence of this country. This is particularly so in the case of radar bases. These were built in very small isolated communities where, to the best of their ability, the people provided the services for the military personnel resident there and participating in community life. We are only asking for a small contribution from the general purse to assist the communities in the one, two or five-year periods when they are winding up their business.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have seconded the motion of the hon. member for Renfrew-Nipissing-Pembroke (Mr. Hopkins). In my opinion, the motion addresses itself in a substantive way to a very real problem which exists from time to time in parts of this country. I think the response of the hon. member for Mississauga North (Mr. Jupp) was nothing more than a bookkeeper's response to a very serious human and social problem that, from time to time, exists in the isolated and less advantaged regions of this country.
In terms of this debate, I am much more in sympathy with the words of the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) who, with myself, shares with these communities the kind of agony and travail that they go through when there is a closure of one kind or another, be it a radar base, a small or large industry. We know, all too well, the sense of crisis that develops whenever this happens.
As my contribution to this debate, I think instead of speaking in generalities 1 should share with the House what could loosely be described as a case study. I lived through the closure of a radar base in a small, unorganized community in a constituency that I represented for more than ten years. It is no longer in my riding, because of the readjustment of the boundary lines. I am referring, of course, to the Canadian forces station at Armstrong, Ontario, a radar station. I know the hon. member for Timiskaming is fully conversant with the problems that existed as a result of that closure. The manner in which it was done can only be described as shameful.
It is true that there was a great deal of good will and a lot of fine intentions displayed by government departments at the time the community was going through this agony. But, sir, good will and fine intentions did not result in any positive action. A $1 million payroll was lost to this small community, and there was no time for adaptation to the change, for adjustment to the new situation. Civilian employees of the Department of National Defence who did not want to move or could not move, were left without jobs. Those who were prepared to move and had relatively inexpensive housing in Armstrong were asked to go to some other part of Canada.

October 29, 1979
Municipal Taxes
They were not provided with a house for a house, so it was just beyond their economic capacity to accept.
In brief, the closing of that radar base was done in a manner which, I would suggest, was not at all an example of good corporate citizenship. It was a public sector enterprise. No one argues about the fact that technology had overtaken the radar base and closure had to come, but the manner in which it took place should have set a good example for private companies which, due to various circumstances and conditions, must sometimes close their operations. The Department of National Defence was sympathetic. The member of Parliament had a good hearing with senior officials in the Department of Defence, with the minister, and with the parliamentary secretary who now sits near me. 1 refer to the hon. member who moved this motion. The Department of National Defence was primarily concerned about its own costs and its own personnel as well as the civilians who were being affected. There was not much they could do, however, because what had to be done was beyond their authority and competence. The Department of Regional Economic Expansion was also involved in a very serious way, and was prepared to assist if a clear-cut proposal with accurate cost estimates was put forward. This did not happen. The department endeavoured to do what it could but, in the end, there was no action they could take.
Ontario Hydro, another agency of government, was willing to consider putting in a power line to replace the diesel power produced by the radar base that had provided electricity for the citizens. They could not do it on their own, however, They needed the pulp companies to throw in some money. They needed the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development to add something and, as well, they needed something from the CNR which was producing power of its own. There were varying degrees of interest, but none of the parties offered the money that was required.
The Crown Assets Disposal Corporation became involved in a rather interesting way. There was a snow plough and a fire truck that this little unorganized community needed, and which DND was prepared to transfer to Crown Assets, so that they somehow could come into the possession of the community. Crown Assets presented a formula which provided that the community could have these two pieces of equipment if it was prepared to pay market value for them. That sounded logical. My bookkeeping friend over there would ask, what is wrong with that? What was wrong with it was that the community of Armstrong was an unorganized municipality. It had no tax base, no revenue. It could not manufacture the money out of thin air. On their behalf 1 put a counter-offer forward. I thought we could raise at least 10 per cent of the market value if Crown Assets was prepared to accept that. They finally did.
Meanwhile, however, the Department of National Defence had second thoughts. They felt they could use this beat up, secondhand, worn out equipment somewhere else, and sent in a couple of military personnel to pick it up. In the middle of a busy afternoon, I received a phone call advising me that two military personnel had come to take away the snow plow and

the fire truck. 1 was asked what I could do about it. There was only one thing that could be done, Mr. Speaker. There was only one road into the town, and with the co-operation of the Ontario Provincial Police a roadblock was set up. The equipment was not allowed to leave until I had the opportunity of speaking to a general or two. They said there had been some kind of misunderstanding, some sort of error, and that the equipment was to remain there. The Ontario Provincial Police took down the roadblock and then provided a police escort to the military personnel so that they could get out of town safely. These are some of the absurd situations and problems that were caused by this kind of a poorly thought out closure of a radar base.
There are many other problems I could cite in this case study, but let me tell the House about the response of an hon. Tory minister in the provincial government. He said that we should not be bothered with all of these problems related to unorganized communities. What we should do is bite the bullet, and let these communities die. Mind you, he did not go to a public meeting in Armstrong and make that statement. He made it in the safety of Queens Park in Toronto. To the best of my knowledge he has never gone to that community.
These small unorganized communities, as the hon. member for Timiskaming knows, do not die. They often have serious economic set backs. They go through a crisis when some job-creating industry or other public or private enterprise leaves, but they do not die. They just linger on and suffer, and the people are a little poorer and worse off for it. But one cannot, by any kind of government action, cause the death of these communities.
What do these communities need? They need a plan for future development. They need someone in these times of crises to help them out. Many government departments, agencies, and even the private sector should get involved. For example, a representative on behalf of one private company said, "We think we can help this community get over this difficulty that it is facing. ' But when a wood cutting operation was started up it was found that adequate accommodations were not available for the workers. It was not possible to attract new skilled labour into the town because facilities were few, if they existed at all.
My hon. friend has proposed that there be a modest program of assistance for these kinds of communities to help them over difficult times. We are not talking about some large, new social program added to our present structure. Of course not. We are all aware of deficits, and we are concerned about them at the various levels of government. But certain expenditures can be justified if there is a real human problem and social need in play, or if it has something to do with nation building or maintaining.
I suggest in addition to what my hon. friend has proposed to this House that there ought to be a co-ordinating committee of government and private enterprise to help communities in crisis overcome these difficulties. Many agencies of govern-
October 29, 1979

ment could be involved. The co-ordinating committee could apply itself with determination and expertise in helping "one industry-small town-unorganized communities" face the crisis of a closure. 1 would think that such a co-ordinating committee should be activated by an order in council. Having assessed the situation, one minister could be designated to press the button in cabinet which would get the committee functioning. It does not need to be a continuing committee or a big costly operation, but it could exist interdepartmentally and include people from the private sector so that when such a problem comes into existence, an order in council could be made to establish and give authority to a committee to help these communities.
1 conclude by saying that what my friend, the hon. member for Renfrew-Nipissing-Pembroke, has proposed is an admirable motion. I am delighted to support it. It is a step in the right direction, and I hope it will have the approval of the House.

I find it a privilege to come here, but having served a goodly number of years in matters of local administration and having served on local government, I find it preferable to address myself to matters of debate of a specific nature.
Local government is an area of government where many of us here have served people of communities for many years in a variety of ways. 1 come here with the full intent, having once served the people of my community, of now addressing myself to the Canadian community, and addressing myself from wherever I sit or stand in what 1 consider the national interest.
1 am somewhat inclined to sympathize with the proponents of this motion, but it is rather ironic it comes before us at a time when Bill C-3 is on the order paper. Bill C-3 is about to
Municipal Taxes
make major changes in the program of grants in lieu of taxes.
1 suggest to all members of this House that that bill will be of benefit to local municipalities. There is no doubt in my mind, Mr. Speaker, that the impact as presented by the proponents of the bill, does change one's lifestyle.
Those who have had to meet budgetary requirements within time periods know what changes come about when there is a change in the assessment rolls by reason of a discontinuance of a major activity, be it an industry, or an institution of governmental change. But that institution came to the municipality concerned, as has already been said, practically at the urging of the municipality. While it leaves an impact, there is no good reason why the federal government should be locked in and be subject to rules and regulations not applicable to other taxpayers or grantors in their particular areas.
May 1 be so bold as to suggest to the hon. member for Renfrew-Nipissing-Pembroke (Mr. Hopkins) that he might better be advised to address himself to Bill C-3 and the Municipal Grants Act when that bill is being discussed before the committee.
The existing program of grants to municipalities in lieu of property taxes is already a substantial item to this country of ours, amounting to about $148 million in the case of department-owned property, and an added $110 million from Crown corporations.
Under the new government bill, grants on departmental properties will be increased by $25 million by bringing into the grant program properties which are now excluded from the grant formula. This will benefit many municipalities across the country and it is a measure that 1 am sure will be supported by all members present.
This particular motion is unusual in that one of the parts of the country that will benefit most from this bill is the constituency of the hon. member for Renfrew-Nipissing-Pembroke. The federal government has a large defence base there, namely Canadian Forces Base Petawawa. At the present time, grants on this base apply to married quarters and land. Bill C-3 will remove this restriction and allow a larger tax base and for a larger grant in lieu thereof.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 was talking about the fact that the Conservative Speech from the Throne was very empty when it came to policy on matters related to energy and the economy. 1 was saying that one reason the Minister of Finance (Mr. Crosbie) has not been able to bring down his own budget as yet is because he does not know what the price of energy will be. He has been hinting that a budget will be presented in November, but today the Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) seemed to suggest, during the question period, that he was hoping for a budget by the end of the year. This would mean further delay when what is needed is prompt action to strengthen the Canadian economy.
In the field of energy prices, the action the Minister of Finance appears to favour is one which, in my view, would harm the Canadian economy rather than help it. He seems to

be promoting a rapid increase to world levels of energy prices in Canada, which would mean increases to $1.30 or $1.40 a gallon for gasoline, an increase of four dollars a barrel for petroleum. All this means an increase of at least 2 per cent in the Canadian cost of living which is already being pushed upward by the Conservative high interest rate policy.
I was informed just before the House resumed that even Premier Lougheed, who at one time was considered such a close friend and supporter of the Prime Minister and his party, has complained, in Vancouver, I believe, about this high interest policy saying, if I recall correctly, that it was a short-term expedient not in the interest of the Canadian economy. The rapid increase in energy prices to world levels apparently sought by the Conservatives would take away most, if not all, of the competitive advantage Canadian industry now possesses when it comes to selling goods both here and abroad because they are able to pay for what are, after all, Canada's own energy resources at prices lower than world prices.
The minister today tabled his mortgage tax credit plan. 1 think we have to recognize that his high interest rate policy, the Conservative high interest rate policy, will cancel out whatever benefit people might have expected from it. It is not the plan which he and the Conservatives promised before the election. A lot of people will get less than they had expected from the old plan. He has admitted, though, that the present tax credit plan is simpler and fairer to lower and middle income people than the one promised by his party before and during the election. We shall, of course, be discussing this matter in greater detail, hopefully within the next few weeks. As 1 have said, though, the Conservative plan promised not simply to help people keep pace with the high Conservative interest rates-which it will not succeed in doing, anyway. People got the impression before and during the election that the Conservative promise of deductibility of mortgage interest rates and property taxes would make them better off than they were at the time that promise was made. But the high interest rates cancel out the benefits completely.
In spite of what the Conservatives said about the budget measures presented to us today during the budget debate last fall, in presenting these measures again they are confirming their value, they are endorsing them, and they are admitting so far they have nothing better. We in the official opposition will therefore not extend debate unduly. We shall, however, insist that the Minister of Finance note and explain clearly what changes, if any, he is making in these measures as compared with what was in the original budget. Our main objective, though, is to have the Minister of Finance present his own budget because action further to what was outlined in the budget of last November can and should be taken in a new budget to help the Canadian economy to make industry more productive and efficient as part of an industrial strategy, as well as measures to help specific sectors of society, for example, small business, farmers, consumers, lower income groups. We in the official opposition will continue to press for measures of this kind.
October 29, 1979

Let the Minister of Finance bring down his own Conservative budget. When it comes, like everything else since the new government took office, there will be a lot less in it than the Conservatives promised the public and the public expected from them before and during the election.

I think we should want to ask ourselves what we are doing to our tax system when we allow the kinds of changes and developments which are so favoured by the government. When 1 listen to the hon. member for Windsor West, 1 am reminded that just as there were two kinds of Tories before the election-there were red Tories and blue Tories-we now find that there are two kinds of Liberals.

speechtext:
There are black Liberals and grey Liberals. The black Liberals are those who thought that what governor

Bouey did was right up until May 22, and they have to agree that what he did was right after May 22. The black Liberals are those who are prepared to admit that they followed the same advice of governor Bouey up until May 22 and that they are prepared to carry the can and support governor Bouey after May 22. While I disagree and have disagreed with the hon. member for Saint-Maurice, the hon. member for Stor-mont-Dundas (Mr. Lumley) and the hon. member for Saint-Henri-Westmount (Mr. Johnston), I at least have some respect for their consistency. I at least know that they will not have worked with the governor of the Bank of Canada, accepted his policies and philosophy for many long years, and then turn around and stab him in the back.
However, the politics of some other Liberals whom 1 have described as grey Liberals are not so consistent. They are very selective in the Liberal tradition which they decide to present to the House as being the new, revised, reformed, revivified, and enlightened Liberal party that they would now have us believe is going to lead Canada to halcyon days.
The problem with the Liberal party is that it is not at the moment an opposition; it is a government in exile. It has not lost that sense that it has, deep in its members' hearts, that somehow on May 22 the Canadian people made a terrible mistake, that all they have to do is snap their fingers and wake up and this horrible nightmare will be over, and once again those who are fit to rule will be ruling over Canada.
