speechtext:
They will have to declare themselves as to whether they are black or grey.
I want to look at the measures put forward by the Conservative party and the Liberal party in an effort to solve our country's economic problems. Let me suggest that our country's economic problems are many. Our prospects and our chances for the future are also many. We in my party have been criticized for being too negative, for being too carping, for being constantly critical, and for not looking at the positive side of things.
Let me say that the pessimists in this House and in this country are not those social democrats who have a conviction that Canadians can do better, that Canadians deserve more and that we have tremendous capacity and strength in our country. The pessimists are those like the hon. member for

October 29, 1979
Income Tax Act
Saint-Maurice when he was minister of finance, and like the current Minister of Finance (Mr. Crosbie), or those people who say there is nothing we can do. What I have described is the weatherman theory of politics and economics; that really what we elect a government to do is to tell us to batten down the hatches and that there is nothing we can do about these natural hurricanes which are taking place throughout the economy.
1 think there are two points which need to be made about our economic problems. The first is that they are structural and serious and that they cannot be solved overnight. The second point to make about our economic problems is that their solution must be fair and be seen to be fair by the Canadian people. In our tax policies, in our interest rate policies-in what are called our fiscal and monetary policies- the Canadian people from Newfoundland to British Columbia must have the sense that they are not being taken advantage of by the powerful and that there is in our tax system an element of fairness which pervades that system.
There is much talk these days about biting the bullet, about austerity, and about how to fight inflation, and I say to hon. members opposite in the Conservative party that all of us in this House and all of us in the country are prepared to fight inflation. The critical question which we continue to put to the government is; who will bear the cost?
The interest rate policy is a redistribution of wealth by another name. It has that effect. It has that impact. It is that unfair, and just as we criticize the interest rate policy because it is unfair, because it does nothing to solve our long-term problems, because it does not deal with the fairness problem and because it does not deal with the structural problems of our economy, so too these tax measures which have been left to us by the previous Liberal government do nothing to face these problems of fairness and structural change. That is why for the most part we are opposed to them, and that is why we have put forward suggestions as to how they should be changed. That is why we will be making what 1 hope the minister will agree are constructive comments having to do with the way these programs have been implemented.
We deal, first of all, with the investment tax credit and the research and development tax credit. There is a basic question which the previous Liberal government was asked several times and which, I suggest, we will be asking this government as well. That basic question is: what is the integrity of our tax system when it is so filled with loopholes, with special provisions, with exceptions, with advantages given to some groups and disadvantages to other groups so that it has no integrity? Indeed, it can be argued that it has even lost its capacity as a revenue collecting system; it is leaking like a sieve, and members opposite know it very well. That is at least three quarters of the reason why we have a deficit that is as large and as uncontrolled as the one we currently have.
When you look at the investment tax credits that have been given, when you look at the mining and drilling allowance that

has been given, when you look at the artificially high rate at which certain industries are allowed to write off capital cost allowance, when you look at the other havens that have been created, you realize that not only do we have a system that is unfair, but we also have a system that is ineffective.
It is to these two points, the fairness and the effectiveness of our tax system, that I think members opposite might address some of their attention. 1 had hoped the Minister of Finance would have addressed some of his attention to them.
What has been the experience with the investment tax credit? Where are the studies to tell us whether these are the incentives which in fact rather than in theory lead to greater investment? Is this spending of public money-because every loss of revenue from a credit is as much a spending of public moneys as if the government wrote a cheque-having the effect that it should have? Is it encouraging regional development? The answer is, no. We have tried the tax credit route, it has been used before by past Liberal governments, and study after study over the last two years has told us that the regional tensions in our country are greater than ever before, that the disparity between the Atlantic provinces and Alberta, for example, is far greater than it was before.
1 think we are entitled to ask ourselves: are these kinds of regional tax credits really the reason why businessmen decide to invest in a certain part of the country rather than in another? Do they simply go to companies that would have invested there anyway and, if so, why are we spending that much money? Is that an effective use of government money? I would have thought that those members opposite who pride themselves on cost effectiveness might want to ask themselves that very simple question, and 1 am glad to see that the Minister of Finance has agreed to bring forward a system of tax spending which will allow us at least to start on the road toward looking at the tax spending system in our country and at how it is attacking the integrity of our tax collecting system and of the revenue capacity of the federal government.
So the question we ask ourselves with respect to the investment tax credit and the research and development tax credit is quite a simple one. Is this adequate? Is this the way to redistribute investment in this country? If that is what the government wants to do, why not do it directly? Why not establish an investment fund? Why not have a national investment strategy? We have asked these questions before, and the Liberals were not able to give us an answer. If the Minister of Finance is serious in what he said earlier today that he wanted to start the country on the long road to national economic independence-this was implied in his remarks-I suggest to him that the way to do this is not by taking the route of giving a handout to every company which comes along and asks for one, or every company which uses the route of the tax credit which cannot be controlled or surveyed, but by using this means to direct investment in our country and to encourage the growth of regions as well as to discourage the amount of regional disparity which we have seen in our country.
There are three other measures to which I want to devote a little time. The first is the drilling allowance. The drilling
October 29, 1979

allowance is, without question, the biggest loophole in our tax system at present. It is a national disgrace because it means- last year we did not have the exact amount for it but we hope the government will give it to us-that the federal government is paying for virtually all frontier oil and gas exploration and is not getting a penny in return.
It means that, for example, Dome Petroleum has not paid a single cent of tax since it was founded some ten years ago. It means Shell Canada did not pay a single penny of tax last year. It means that while this government is screwing up its courage, to quote Shakespeare, to fight PetroCan which cost the public treasury somewhere between $300 million and $400 million, it is, at the same time, handing out money hand over fist to the oil companies, which is bad enough and stupid enough, without getting a penny of equity or of interest, or of guarantee of an interest in the long run for the Canadian taxpayer. This is the kind of "tough bargaining" which we can expect from the Liberals, but we hope for a better deal for the Canadian taxpayer from the Conservatives.
Not only that, it means also that the allowance and the loopholes go to those wealthy investors who are encouraged to shelter their money in a frontier drilling allowance. There are not many people in my riding who can afford even to know about or be aware of the meaning of a tax shelter like the frontier drilling allowance, but 1 think the meaning of these shelters should become crystal clear to the Canadian taxpayers. Not only are we subsidizing the takeover of our frontier resources by foreign multinational oil companies so that we are paying people to buy us out, it also means that we are paying wealthy Canadians to reap benefits from the exploration of resources. It means at the same time that while this is going on and while this unfairness is filtering through our tax system, the Conservative party has decided to pick on poor old PetroCan, the one foot in the door which the Canadian public has in the resource sector, in the oil exploration sector, and to give it back to the private sector as well.

subsubtopic: MEASURETO AMEND
speechtext: Shame!

subsubtopic: MEASURETO AMEND
speechtext:
The hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Breau) says it is shameful. I ask him to look at the drilling allowance system which has been set up in the country. I ask him to look at frontier allowance shelters and to go back to his constituents and tell them how fair they are. That is what the Liberal government stood for, and he knows perfectly well if he went back to his constituents and told them about it, they would shake their heads in disbelief. 1 think people are entitled to know about it.
The second point is one that was already mentioned by the Minister of Finance, and that is the change in the term "preferred shares". Both inside and outside this House many members of our party have made the point that, even after the loophole has been closed, our banks are paying virtually no tax. The Minister of Finance says that is not true, he does not agree with my theories. He said the NDP is the party of the twenty-first century. I would remind the minister that the twenty-first century is only 20 years away. I would rather be in
Income Tax Act
the party of the twenty-first century than the party of the eighteenth century.
When one looks at what has happened to term preferred shares, one realizes that although the door has been closed, the horse has already bolted. Even as we are in the third quarter of 1979, the average rate of taxation of the banks is 10.7 per cent. I think Canadians are entitled to an explanation. 1 look forward to an explanation from the minister. I look forward to him telling us what he is going to do. The hon. member for Saint-Maurice closed the loophole long after it had the effect of allowing an extraordinary benefit not only to the banks but to those large companies which took advantage of the system. Because the arrangements have been made, because they were entered into, and because the system of term preferred shares lasts on an average between six years and eight years, we have a long way to go before we will collect the taxes which have not been collected as a result of this device.
I think we are entitled to indicate that the door has been closed and the horse is long gone, thanks to the negligence and ignorance of the Liberal government, thanks to its lack of concern for the integrity of the tax system, thanks to its lack of concern for the fairness of the tax system. The question which Canadian taxpayers will be asking members of the House of Commons is: what will be done about it now that the horse is gone?
Finally we come to the one feature of the budget on which the minister wanted to put his own particular stamp. He wanted to make it a Conservative measure as well as a Liberal one. I have only described some of the unfairness in the budget. In addition is the fact that it did not provide for the personal tax cut which obviously was needed back in 1978. The Minister of Finance went a little further, but it is interesting that the only major change the Tories chose to make was to give high income professionals a tax break. It was given to high income professionals, not to the man in the street.

subsubtopic: MEASURETO AMEND
speechtext: What about the woman in the street?

subsubtopic: MEASURETO AMEND
speechtext:
It was not given to the person in the street. It was given to lawyers, doctors, and dentists, who are in positions where they can incorporate themselves. By the magic of incorporation, they can reduce their effective tax rate to 25 per cent. It is this illusion of unfairness that at least the Liberals realized created abuse. A special tax rate for small business was not created to give a ripoff to professionals. It was not to allow them to avoid taxes. It was not so that they would not be treated like everyone else in the tax system. It was in order to give a benefit to those people who will be going out and hiring people to start a small business and get the economy moving. That is why there was this 25 per cent rate.
Presto, what has the minister done? He said that the way they were going to change this was to switch it from a 25 per cent rate to a 33 per cent rate. The minister has said that this has a neutral tax effect, but I think he is kidding the Canadian

October 29, 1979
Income Tax Act
public, and the figures will show it. The minister is kidding the Canadian public because it will not have a neutral tax effect.
The tax effect will be that professionals and members of their families, however they devise it and plan it through their tax planning arrangements for those family members who are engaged in so-called service arrangements with the doctors and so forth, will have far lower effective rates of taxation than if they were not able to take advantage of the incorporation loophole.
I think Canadians are entitled to know that the only thing the members of the Conservative caucus successfully pressured the Minister of Finance on was a tax cut for professionals, not a tax cut for all Canadians, not a means of helping lower and middle income people who are being shafted by high interest rates, not a means of helping pensioners who are struggling to make ends meet. The one group of Canadians whom this government decided to single out in its first act before Parliament by saying, "You people really need help", were the lawyers, doctors and dentists. They singled out high income professionals who are doing very well. Surely, in the name of goodness, they do not deserve the first break, the first act of charity and kindness to come out of the Conservative government.
I think Canadians expected something a little different and better than they received from the government. I will not engage in the kind of hypocritical criticism which we have heard from the government in exile, the Liberal party. Consistently we have opposed the unfairness of Liberal tax measures, the loopholes which have almost become synonymous with Liberal tax measures and the tremendous benefits to the multi-national oil companies which we have described. We say the same thing to the Conservative government, the tight money second team as I described them earlier.
We expected something different from the tight money second team than we have received so far. The people to whom they made promises during the election, those Canadians who remember that the Conservatives in their ridings promised a tax break, will be wondering why they did not receive the same tax breaks as lawyers, doctors and dentists. 1 do not think the government will have an answer for them. The government is responding to those same special interest groups, those same people who think giving a few more breaks to those who have will somehow stimulate the economy and that they will convince every other Canadian that what is happening is fair.
One message will come back and haunt the government. Not only does it have to deal with structural problems of the economy, it will not have Canadians behind it unless they are satisfied that everybody in society will be bearing the burden, and that not only doctors, lawyers and dentists will be receiving a little relief. It cannot deal with structural problems of the economy with a high interest rate and a laissez-faire government which leaves everything to multi-national companies. Canadians will have to be satisfied that pensioners, industrial workers, clerical workers, persons with a little education, and those persons who do not have enough get up and go to start a business, according to Conservative philosophy, will receive
[Mr. Rae.[
equal benefit. They deserve just as much a break and just as much fairness from the tax system as doctors, lawyers, dentists, chartered accountants, and insurance salesmen, who are so beloved by the Conservative party and the Conservative government.
The Liberal budget is worthy of the Liberal party. The black and grey Liberals can unite on this one. I am afraid it is worthy of what we have come to expect so far from the Conservative party which has ignored the great traditions of a national policy, but it is not something which is worthy of the House taken as a whole. We will be putting forward amendments during consideration of it in Committee of the Whole. We will be opposing these benefits because we think that they provide too great a share of the national wealth to a few Canadians. We will be asking that this government demonstrate two things: economic leadership, and compassion. A party which does not combine economic leadership and compassion will very soon find that it is out of favour with the Canadian people. I hope that those so-called "blue Tories" on the other side of the House remember what 1 have said because, if they do not, it will come back to haunt them.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to be in the House tonight and to have this opportunity to enter into this debate. It is interesting to follow the comments of the financial critics for the Liberal party and for the NDP. The financial critic for the NDP was not here on May 23, 1978, but the whole day was spent debating a review of the tax structure for Canada. My party wanted to refer the matter to committee, but this was criticized by the Liberal party which, assisted by the NDP, talked this motion out. The two opposition parties were no more interested in reviewing the tax structure then than they are now.
It is a full-time job to keep up with the statements made by the New Democratic Party members, particularly their statements about what oil companies pay with regard to taxes. Of course, I have another statement which I will have to check out tomorrow, that being the statement by the NDP financial critic that Dome Petroleum does not pay taxes. That statement is probably just as false as all the other statements which they have made and which I will be reading into the record tonight.
There has also been discussion on the high interest rates. I will be going into some detail later in my speech as to why we have these terribly high interest rates. It has nothing to do with policies which my government has introduced, it is simply that we are forced to pay off the Liberal debt. I shall be going into these figures in a moment to remind the Liberal financial critic of the debt his government left this Canadian nation and how it trapped the Canadian people. One of the reasons why we must have these high interest rates is to attract money to pay off the Liberal debt. I will be going into the exact figures.
The financial critic of the NDP has made statements to the effect that all my party is interested in are professional people. That is not true. We have introduced legislation to deal with
October 29, 1979

veterans, pensions, spouse's allowance, and aid has been granted to the municipalities in lieu of taxes, to mention but a few. The Liberal party has continuously criticized our tax credit plan for homeowners. If it is so interested in homeowners, it could have implemented this policy in 1965 because that is when my party first proposed the idea. However, at that time all we got from the Liberal government were taxes on building products. It is no more interested in home owners than it is in flying to the moon.
The Liberal financial critic was held in high esteem in the last Parliament, after he was removed from cabinet. He was quite credible in the House, and the hon. member asked many pointed questions of the government at that time. But now that the hon. member is a critic he seems to have a convenient memory. I would like to remind the hon. member of a bill which his party introduced on January 27, 1978, to bring Canada's oil up to world prices. They have since reversed their stand on this policy, but there has been no explanation as to why. As yet, this government has not said anything about bringing our oil up to world prices because we have not reached a final decision as to what the price will be. The then minister of energy, mines and resources is reported as saying in Hansard at page 2313, January 27, 1978 with regard to his Bill C-19:
The principal purpose of this bill is to enable the government to fulfil its commitment to provide international prices for the synthetic oil produced-
Then he goes on to say:
Steps which have already been taken by the government include the following:
1. A commitment to move Canadian oil prices toward international levels in order to encourage conservation and resource development.
If that party has changed its mind and its policy, 1 would like it to give an explanation, and never mind its negative criticism about what the government is doing with regard to oil prices. Similar comments can be found throughout this debate which carried on until April 10, 1978, where the Liberal party said that it would bring Canadian oil prices up to world prices.
I would like to give the House and hon. members present some idea of what my government has inherited from the successive Liberal governments which can only be described as the most irresponsible group of individuals to have ever held public office in Canadian history. The expenditures in main estimates for the fiscal year 1979-80 are $52.6 billion; for 1980-81, $57.95 billion; for the fiscal year 1981-82, $63.85 billion, and for 1982-83 $69.9 billion. The party while it was in power absolutely trapped the Canadian people. The budget will rise by $20 billion in three years without the present government bringing in one single spending program. They have put in motion this uncontrolled spending, and that is the problem. We must try to reduce that $70 billion budget, and that is why we cannot give tax cuts to renters or the small businessmen. We would like to give more support to the veterans and other groups, but the veterans, renters, home owners and businessmen must pay off this huge expenditure.

net public debt was $51.5 billion. This has all been set in motion by the Liberal government, and the net public debt could reach $104,710 billion by 1983. He simply offers negative criticism and a complete reversal of policy. It is the policies of the Liberal government which have caused the high interest rates, and I hope that we can overcome this situation. The tax rate for the oil industry declined from 35 per cent to 21 per cent.
He-

There has been widespread concern expressed by a number of Canadians over the future of PetroCan. But there has also been widespread misunderstanding on all sides concerning the Conservative government's proposals in this regard. Much of the misunderstanding has been fostered by those groups who do not understand the poor condition of PetroCan in its present form, or the government's proposals.

May 1 begin by saying it is not the intention of this government to privatize or sell PetroCan to foreign interests. Nor is it our intention-in any sense-to weaken the Crown corporation.
Rather, the government intends to strengthen Canada's role in the oil industry. In order to achieve this-a goal which every Canadian wants-PetroCan must first be reorganized. In its present condition, the Crown corporation is a weak company in a very healthy industry. Despite the propaganda campaign being waged by the NDP and Liberal parties, PetroCan, in its present form, is not protecting Canada's interests in the oil industry.
I am enclosing additional information for my constituents.
The letter goes on:
An overview of the highlights of the task force's report will show how a restructed PetroCan will better serve Canada in a way the present corporation is unable.
First, a reorganized PetroCan would be owned by all Canadians and would consist of about 95 per cent of the assets of the present corporation. After initial distribution, only Canadians would be permitted to purchase any freely traded shares. The amount of equity held by any Canadian or corporation would be limited within strict bounds.
Whether we are going to implement that, I do not know, but that is being considered at the present time.
The letter continues:
Secondly, and just as important, the new corporation would no longer be in chronic debt. In the first six months of 1979, PetroCan has lost $7.6 million. Since it began operation in 1976, the federal government has pumped $800 million worth of equity capital into the corporation. Its financial structure as it now exists is overburdened with debt. Debt exceeds 250 per cent of equity versus the ratio of between 25 per cent and 40 per cent of other petroleum companies.
Now we have the Liberal party and the New Democratic Party supporting a Crown corporation that has a debt equity of 250 per cent. They go around telling the Canadian people what a wonderful company it is because of a debt ratio like that. I do not think they understand what a debt ratio is.

Through the proposed reorganization, with the debt of the privatized part largely removed, the new company could earn Canadian shareholders in excess of $100 million per year while the debt of the government would be reduced by about $300 million.
Third, the new corporation will retain three essential functions now performed by PetroCan. The corporation will retain the function of negotiating state to state contracts for crude oil;-

-exploration in frontier areas; and the development of tar sands. The retention of these three functions, along with a largely debt-free corporation owned by all Canadians, would ensure Canada has strong voice in the energy field.
Finally, the new corporation would, under the proposed reorganization, be more aggressive in the oil industry.
Instead of merely providing money for other operators, such as Mobil, in their explorations, the new company will be a leader in the field of exploration. Unlike the present corporation which has yet to drill an oil well of its own in the frontier areas, the reorganized corporation will surely be a leader in this area.
The Conservative government is as concerned as are all Canadians, of ensuring that Canada has a strong voice in the field of energy. Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to take part in this debate on second reading of Bill C-17, an act to amend the statute law relating to income tax and to amend the Canada Pension Plan. Of course, it is not the wish of this party to prolong this debate unduly because at this stage the House of Commons has to vote on the principle of a bill. So, as the House at this late date, in late October, 1979, is still considering legislative matters arising from the budget of last November, obviously we would not want to delay unduly the legislative process on this bill. But, Mr. Speaker, I think it is important to set certain things straight when dealing with budgetary matters, quite simply because nearly every day during question period the ministers answer
Income Tax Act
questions put to them by saying that if today we have a difficult financial situation, if the governor of the Bank of Canada must constantly increase interest rates-that now stand at 14 per cent-it is because of the financial situation in which this country finds itself, apparently brought about by the Fiberal party, the previous government.
Mr. Speaker, it is an argument that has absolutely no credibility, quite simply because the government officially became the government on June 4. They were elected on May 22 and since June 4, they have waited nearly four and a half months to reconvene the House of Commons, contrary, as my colleague for Windsor West (Mr. Gray) pointed out this afternoon, to the practice in effect previously in Canada and in other countries like Great Britain, for example. When a new government gets a new mandate, one of the first things it must do is to call the Houses, summon Parliament and bring forward its economic policy and legislative program.
Here is a Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) who suggests they had no data, they did not know what they were talking about, they knew nothing of Canada's economic affairs, and therefore they needed training. This is in effect what the Prime Minister said this afternoon. He indicated that when he spoke in this House last year, when the financial critics-because there were many-Mr. Gillies and the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Stevens), the then hon. member for York-Simcoe, both were financial critics. I remember very well that in November last, during the budget debate, he started referring to the situation and exaggerating the Canadian deficit. He was referring to figures in the order of $25 billion or $30 billion a year, because at that time he obviously wanted to scare Canadians. He wanted to exaggerate the economic situation, pretending it was very bad.
How can the government now tell us they did not know what this country's economic situation was, when at the time they were the opposition they did not stop referring during last year's budget debate to this country's grave difficulties? Mr. Speaker, they knew what the economic situation was.
They knew last year that the policy they were advocating, the famous $2 billion tax cut, was completely irresponsible. They knew at that time that the monetary policy they were suggesting for supporting the dollar at 90 cents or 92 cents was absolutely irresponsible. In the last two or three weeks the dollar has gone down on the market. We have not heard the Progressive Conservatives complain and say that this is terrible and that the value of the dollar should be brought up to 90 cents or 92 cents.
Mr. Speaker, the members opposite must realize that they have lost all their credibility and that they are acting completely irresponsibly simply because they did not tell the truth to the Canadian population last year during the election campaign, and are not telling the truth now. They should stop groping about for solutions and bring down a budget. It is really regrettable that at the end of October, with a new

government which was elected in May and which officially took power on June 4, we have not yet passed a single bill. We are now at the end of October, Mr. Speaker. Mr. Speaker, the excuses given by this government to justify its unwillingness to present a budget now cannot be taken seriously. The Minister of State for International Trade (Mr. Wilson) could tell us about the problems within the government; he might explain why we lost the contract with

Argentina, a $2 billion contract that might cost us even more just because the ministers were unable to make decisions. Will we continue to carry out idealistic policies or are we going to be more practical? The government could not make up its mind last summer.

Does the Progressive Conservative Party have any policy about oil prices? If it has one, is it ready to put it into effect? Suddenly there was no more problem among producing and consuming provinces. Mr. Speaker, it has become obvious that so far this government has failed miserably to get an agreement on oil prices. There again, we can see that they were not being responsible when they were criticizing us for the unilateral measures the then federal government had to take on oil prices. Premier Hatfield of New Brunswick, Premier MacLean of Prince Edward Island, Mr. Levesque of the province of Quebec, Mr. Peckford of Newfoundland and Mr. Buchanan of Nova Scotia will say, "Raise the price of oil because that will increase the revenues of Alberta and, consequently, those of my province through the equalization system." There are some basic problems which the Canadian economy faces. Average Canadian workers and income earners know this better than anybody else. The small business tax rate has been a subject of extensive public discussion over the past, and the proposals of the previous government have been widely criticized. Under the proposals introduced in the November, 1978, budget, the benefits of the special corporate tax rate on small business would have been denied to three categories of small business income. They were professional income, the income from certain personal services, and the income from the provision of certain management and other administrative services. Under these proposals, these types of business income would have been taxed at the normal rate of corporate taxation of between 46 per cent and 51 per cent depending on the province, rather than at the special rate of 25 per cent for small business.
This clause of the bill introduces a new small business tax rate of 3316 per cent for any Canadian-controlled private company engaged in any of the three categories of business previously described. For this purpose the professional group, which originally included doctors, dentists, lawyers and accountants, will be expanded to include veterinarians and chiropractors.

This deferral would not have been possible under the proposals of the last government. In addition, the new rules will be reflected in the law rather than in the regulations. The changes will apply to taxation years commencing after 1979 for corporations in existence on October 23, 1979, and to all taxation years for corporations formed after today.
Since all Canadian business income, other than investment income, of the three categories of corporations affected by the change will be subject to the 3316 per cent small business tax rate, such corporations will be given time to re-arrange their affairs so that they can receive the benefit of the lower small business tax rate on eligible active business income. Because some companies may be unable to re-arrange their affairs before the end of the year, the President of the Privy Council and Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Baker) has indicated that he will be prepared to allow corporations, which wish to reorganize in light of these amendments, to change their fiscal year ends in 1980. No significant changes will be made to the rules proposed by the previous government relating to the treatment of investment income for purposes of small business deductions.
In regard to detailed comments, prior to 1972 a low tax rate of 21 per cent on the first $35,000 of corporate income was available. While the low rate on the first $35,000 was described as an incentive to small business, it was available to all corporations regardless of the type of income they earned, regardless of whether they were expanding or static, regardless of whether they were Canadian or foreign-controlled, or owned by public corporations or private individuals.
To more specifically target the benefits derived from a low tax rate, the current structure of the small business deduction was introduced with tax reform in 1972 in place of the previous measure. In order to focus more accurately on individual Canadian entrepreneurship, the measure was restricted to Canadian-controlled private corporations. In order to direct the benefits to smaller Canadian-controlled companies, the measure now applies to Canadian source business income of a corporation, as long as the corporation's accumulated business earnings net of dividends paid do not exceed $750,000.
Section 125 of the Income Tax Act provides for a 21 per cent tax reduction for the Canadian active business income of Canadian-controlled private corporations. This reduction to a 25 per cent basic corporate tax rate from the normal corporate tax rate of 46 per cent is available annually on up to $150,000 of Canadian active business, until such time as the corporation reaches its $750,000 cumulative limit. When this special 25

per cent small business rate was first introduced as part of the tax reform in 1972, the amount of annual income eligible for the low rate was limited to $50,000. Both the annual and cumulative limits have been increased twice since 1972.
The small business tax rate was designed to allow Canadian-controlled firms to accumulate funds for expansion, to allow them to compete against larger firms, and to create jobs for Canadian workers. Accordingly the legislation provides that only income from an active business carried on in Canada be eligible for this favourable tax treatment.
Coupled with these tax reform changes and developments regarding the taxation of small businesses, amendments have been made to the dividend tax credit with the view to reducing further the possibilities of double taxation of corporate source income. The dividend tax credit was made taxable by introducing the concept of a gross-up technique to dividends received by individuals. The purpose of the gross-up is to include in the shareholder's income an amount approximating the pre-tax earnings of the corporation. As a result the dividend tax credit provides tax recognition, in the hands of the individual shareholder, for 25 points of corporate tax, which in turn represents the full amount of corporate income tax paid on business income earned by Canadian-controlled private corporations qualifying for the basic 25 per cent tax rate.
In 1977 the dividend credit was increased from one third to one half of the amount of the dividend. This increase generally enhanced the attractiveness of receiving dividend payments and thereby provided an incentive for making equity investments. Also the change had the desirable effect of bringing the tax on dividends more closely into line with the tax on capital gains.

subtopic: CONSUMER AND CORPORATE AFFAIRS-DISSEMINATION OF INFORMATION GATHERED ON POSSIBLE PROSECUTIONS
CONSUMER AND CORPORATE AFFAIRS-DISSEMINATION OF INFORMATION GATHERED ON POSSIBLE PROSECUTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question at issue is one which arises out of a series of questions and, more specifically, a question which 1 asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) on October 17. The question at issue is important because it involves, in my view, the role of the Attorney General as a law officer of the Crown and the independence of the Attorney General in the exercise of his functions, indeed, as a law officer of the Crown, so that the Attorney General may not only be independent in the exercise of that function, but can be seen to be independent.
The second issue is the independence of the director of investigations as he discharges his responsibilities under the Combines Investigation Act.
There is a series of undisputed facts. There was a meeting which was held on October 12 at eight o'clock a.m. and which was called by the Attorney General of Canada. Attending that meeting were the Minister of Justice, (Mr. Flynn), the Solicitor General and Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Lawrence), the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankow-ski), and the director of investigations as well as sundry officials.
The discussion centred around possible criminal violations under the Combines Investigation Act involving Western Transport Association and Household Goods Corporations. What is also not disputed is that no such meetings had been under the previous administration involving the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and the Attorney General at the time when the Attorney General was contemplating prosecutions under the Combines Investigation Act. Those are the facts which we know.
The facts which we do not know are much more numerous. First of all, what was the purpose of that meeting? Was it to gather information? Was it to provide information? Or was it a forum in order to have parties influence the course of the investigation or the prosecution? What role did the director of investigations play at that meeting? Was it an active role? Was it a reluctant role? What role did the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs play in terms of protecting the director and his independence? Had the director actually submitted his evidence under Section 15 prior to the meeting, or was the meeting intended to head the director of investigations off at the pass so that the Attorney General would not have to make a decision under Section 15 as to whether a prosecution ought to be held?
What role did the Minister of Transport play at that meeting? Was it one of gaining information, or was it one of providing information? There is some dispute about those facts. What was the nature of the brief that was prepared by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs for the benefit of the Minister of Transport which, allegedly, the Minister of Transport never received?
What was the nature of the briefing note prepared by the Minister of Transport's own officials? Was that only to pro-

October 29, 1979

vide him with information, or was it suggestive of his role in preventing a prosecution or in somehow affecting the role of the director? Was there any attempt to interfere with the director's investigation or with the ability of the director to have the Attorney General deal with the matter under Section 15?
Finally, what role did the Attorney General play in this particular meeting? From his own evidence he did not even know what was going to be discussed at that meeting. What representations were made by the Minister of Transport or his officials to the Minister of Justice and the Attorney General? Answers have to be found to all those questions in order to satisfy the House that the independence of the Attorney General was protected.
I wish, Mr. Speaker, to bring to the attention of the House a quotation from a very distinguished jurist relating to the issue of the independence of the Attorney General in matters of prosecution or potential prosecution. This gentleman stated, "1 would say that any consultation would have to be on the legal propriety of the prosecution and not on any other element. It might be, for instance, that some other member of the cabinet might be very experienced in a particular branch of the law involved, in which case he might consult him." That is a very precise indication of the role of the Attorney General as he considers whether he ought to take on a particular prosecution. Mr. Justice Spence is advancing a very interesting argument. I am not saying it is a conclusive argument, but surely that is the sort of debate in which this House has to engage itself.
Next, what about the independence of the director in the discharge of his responsibilities? Was he protected? Was he free at that meeting to advance his own views? Had he discussed the matter with the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs so that that minister, at that meeting, would be aware of the position the director took and so that the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs could protect his director in the face of his cabinet colleagues? Was that investigation completely independent? What we know-

speechtext:
1 am very eager to rise and respond to the question that has been put by the hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. Blais) because 1 hope that, once and for all, we can put an end to the series of red herrings that have been drawn across this chamber in the last few days on this issue. At the same time 1 should like to refresh the hon. member's memory of what the proper practice is with regard to ministerial responsibility on a matter of this kind.
Here, Mr. Speaker, are the essential elements of the position of the Attorney General of Canada in relation to prosecutions under the Combines Investigation Act, and any other act if it comes to that. The director of investigations and research may
Adjournment Debate
bring any matter under inquiry to the attention of the Attorney General under the provisions of Section 13 or Section 15 of the Combines Investigation Act. Section 15 provides that the director may, at any stage of an inquiry, remit evidence to the Attorney General of Canada for consideration, to determine whether an offence has been or is about to be committed, and for such action as the Attorney General may be pleased to take.
In dealing with a case where a matter has been referred to him, the Attorney General is unquestionably entitled to obtain both information and advice from whatever sources he sees fit, including his colleagues in cabinet. The decision he takes in particular cases must, however, in the last analysis, be his decision. The Attorney General does not act on directions from his colleagues, other members of Parliament or anyone else, in discharging his duties in the enforcement of the law. On the other hand, he must be prepared to answer to Parliament for what he has done after he makes his final decision. These principles are well known and established, not only in Canada, but in every common law jurisdiction. I refer particularly to the United Kingdom where the practice, of course, grew up.
I should like to read into the record the best statement on the question that I am aware of, which may be found in a work prepared by Professor Edwards of the University of Toronto entitled "Law Officers of the Crown". I shall give my hon. friend the reference when I finish. Professor Edwards said:
I think the true doctrine is... that it is the duty of an Attorney General, in deciding whether or not to authorize the prosecution, to acquaint himself with all the relevant facts, including, for instance, the effect which the prosecution, successful or unsuccessful as the case may be, would have upon public morale and order, and with any other consideration affecting public policy. In order so to inform himself, he may, although I do not think he is obliged to, consult with any of his colleagues in the government, and indeed, as Lord Simon once said, he would in some cases be a fool if he did not. On the other hand, the assistance of his colleagues is confined to informing him of particular considerations which might affect his own decision, and does not consist, and must not consist, in telling him what that decision ought to be. The responsibility for the eventual decision rests with the Attorney General, and he is not to be put, and is not put, under pressure by his colleagues in the matter. Nor, of course, can the Attorney General shift his responsibility for making the decision on to the shoulders of his colleagues-

EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-MEETING OF HON. ROBERT STANFIELD WITH PLO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, ten days ago I addressed a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Miss MacDonald) concerning the meeting held by the Hon. Robert Stanfield with a representative of PLO terrorists. Specifically I asked whether Mr. Stanfield has held any public or clandestine meetings and, if so, had Mr. Stanfield discussed with that terrorist organization any subject other than, or in addition to, the moving of the embassy from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem, and further had Mr. COMMONS DEBATES
October 29, 1979
Adjournment Debate
Stanfield made any undertakings to continue further contacts with the PLO.
1 do appreciate the opportunity that is afforded in this House to a member to be able to press for an answer to a question which a member feels was not answered during question period.
To set the record straight, it would be unfair for me to imply or allege that the hon. minister did not reply at all, but the answer was not given to my question. My question was not frivolous, and certainly not deserving of delay. It deals with a matter of grave consequences, consequences meaning that Canada may be giving tacit de facto recognition or encouragement to the PLO, which has, as we know, been involved in terrorist activites, killing not only Jewish but Arab civilians, men, women and children in Israel and in many other parts of the world. It also seeks to obliterate the existence of the state of Israel and indirectly some, or even many members of its population.
Let me point out why it is so serious, important and urgent that a reply to my question be given to this House and to the entire country. What perhaps is at stake is our national honour, the imperilling of the peace process in the Middle East, the possibility of alienating friends such as the United States of America, Israel, and others in the international community, and of giving comfort, therefore, encouragement to the PLO terrorists-a totally immoral act for Canada and an unfriendly one toward the friendly state of Israel.
In short, I would still like to know the answer to my question. The implications are even more grave as the truth unravels. First of all, what rank and authority is Mr. Stanfield perceived by other governments to have? We were told here by the Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) on October 12 that Mr. Stanfield is an ambassador extraordinary, and that because of the adjective extraordinary there can be, and I quote, "no implication of official recognition by the Canadian government of any groups with which he may have consultations." Yet today the Prime Minister tabled a letter from Mr. Stanfield to the Prime Minister on official stationery which describes Mr. Stanfield as, and I quote, "Special Representative of the Government of Canada, and Ambassador at Large." Those are very imposing and impressive titles when added up: ambassador extraordinary, special representative of the Government of Canada, and ambassador at large.
I wonder whether in the eyes of governments which are used to these terms as they have been undertsood in international law or customs over the centuries, it is now realized that a new dictionnary has been written by our Prime Minister giving a new definition to those terms.
Mr. Stanfield met with Khalid al-Fahum, chairman of the Palestine National Council, the PLO's governing body, and a member of the PLO executive committee.
It has been claimed that this meeting between Mr. Stanfield and Mr. al-Fahum does not constitute recognition of the PLO by Canada. Arab diplomats and the PLO, however, can easily

interpret such meetings as constituting a form of recognition of the terrorist organization which remains committed to Israel's ultimate destruction. The PLO's covenant, which has not been renounced, calls for the elimination of Israel. More recent statements by the PLO leaders, including the PLO chairman, Yasser Arafat, belie any intention on the part of that body to recognize Israel or to change its goal of its destruction.
I have in my file recent statements by Mr. Arafat, and I quote:
Armed struggle is our only road. We have no other road to reach Jerusalem, Tel Aviv and every inch of our occupied homeland.
Our people will continue to fuel the torch of the revolution with rivers of blood until the whole of the occupied homeland is liberated ... not just a part of it.
I am confident that we shall eventually overrun Begin's own offices in both Jerusalem and Tel Aviv ... Jerusalem is destined to be the eternal capital of our sovereign independent Palestinian state under the PLO leadership.
Mr. Arafat is not referring only to the "liberation" of the West Bank and Gaza. He refers to the entire state of Israel.
A few weeks ago, Farouk Kaddoumi, director of the PLO political department said; "The PLO will never recognize Israel even if Israel recognizes the PLO" Given such a policy, it seems difficult to comprehend why Mr. Stanfield found it necessary or useful to meet with the PLO's representative. The PLO's vision of peace does not include a state of Israel in the Middle East.

Mr. Speaker, this is the first opportunity I have had for an exchange with the hon. member for Eglinton-Lawrence (Mr. de Corneille) whose reputation has preceded him into this House. I wish him well in his parliamentary career. I want to suggest, in dealing with questions as sensitive as the Middle East, that a certain balanced approach is going to be necessary to reflect that objectivity that I know he wants to bring to this House.
When he complains that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Miss MacDonald) did not answer the question that he originally posed, he is overlooking the fact the minister did affirm that Mr. Stanfield met a high representative of the PLO Having detoured us on that, he comes into the House tonight and the burden of his argument is there having been this meeting between Mr. Stanfield and Mr. Khalid al-Fahum, chairman of the Palestine National Council, that implies a tacit recognition of this terrorist organization by the Canadian government and, second, this is imperilling the peace process. In fact, nothing of the kind has resulted from this.
The Palestine National Council is a deliberative body on which are represented various Palestinian organizations as well as individual unaffiliated Palestinians. Mr. Stanfield and Mr. al-Fahum in their discussion concentrated on the Middle East situation in general and in particular the prospects for a negotiated peace, and the role of Palestinians in that process. They also touched on the Jerusalem issue. There was no
October 29, 1979

discussion of whether or how there should be further contacts between the PLO and Canada.
Now we come to the heart of the hon. member's assertion in which he suggested this meeting implied tacit recognition. No meeting of this nature could imply a recognition of the PLO by the Government of Canada. If in fact the PLO is neither a state nor a government and does not claim such a status, how then can formal recognition of such an organization follow from a meeting?
The government did not and does not intend that Mr. Stanfield's meeting with Mr. al-Fahum should constitute any form of official recognition of the PLO as what it claims to be, the sole and legitimate representative of the Palestinians. The circumstances in which the government would be prepared to consider the PLO as speaking with authority for the Palestinian people have been very clearly set out by the Prime Minister. Neither criterion has been satisfied as things now stand.

subtopic: HAZARDOUS PRODUCTS-REMEDIAL ACTION BY CHIP TO PROTECT HOME OWNERS FROM HAZARDOUS INSULATION MATERIALS
HAZARDOUS PRODUCTS-REMEDIAL ACTION BY CHIP TO PROTECT HOME OWNERS FROM HAZARDOUS INSULATION MATERIALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to thank the minister for taking sufficient interest in this topic to appear personally in the House this evening. 1 had asked the hon. gentleman previously about the home insulation program, considering this to be an extremely important program.
All this week we have heard how the cost of oil might go up. We have heard how interest rates are going up and the average consumer will be caught in a tight squeeze. An area in which we can take positive steps to reduce the cost of living is the home insulation program. I was going through my notes and 1 see that in one study done by a group from Princeton University in a town called Twin Rivers in New Jersey, it is claimed that three-quarters of the energy used by furnaces in private homes can be eliminated. There are other statistics which show that the amount of money spent on building a nuclear reactor if spent on home insulation, could save more electricity than a nuclear reactor could ever produce.
Home insulation is inflation proof. It is a way in which we can save billions of dollars in foreign exchange by reducing our imports of oil. It fits in with the trend of a more conserving society-making do with what we have makes so much sense.
There are, however, some serious problems with the program. One CBC program in Winnipeg reported that Manitoba Hydro had done a study of 200 randomly selected homes and found that nearly 90 per cent of them did not reach their full insulation potential. There was a group in Waterloo which conducted thermo-checks using infra-red photography, and found that in over 60 per cent of the homes re-insulation had not been properly carried out.
Adjournment Debate
What are the problems? First there is a problem with materials. Cellulose fibre has been classed as a hazardous material. I asked the minister whether similar tests had been conducted at the time with urea-formaldehyde foam as well as treated wood chips. I understand there are serious problems attached to those materials. I understand the foam gives off a toxic formaldehyde gas if not properly applied. What we have is an industry which has grown very fast in a short period of time. Serious problems have been created by a number of unscrupulous or inexperienced manufacturers of materials. According to one statistic which is floating around 60 per cent of the homes which have been insulated with cellulose fibre in the maritimes will experience rotting of the basic structure. This is because cellulose fibre, if it gets damp, produces a fungus growth leading to a rotting of the structure.
I have received reports from all over the country about fly-by-night operators. They generally prey on elderly people and sell them a bill of goods whereby they get some insulation work done, mostly in the attic, and they are charged $500, which CHIP pays. However, local contractors would charge only $200 or $250 for the same job. There is a serious rip-off happening not only for the consumer but also for the government.
I find some difficulty with the CHIP administration. I feel that this is a problem this government has inherited. The former government prided itself on being able to run a very solid administration, but CHIP is just an administrative disaster. It is not living up to the potential the money put into it would indicate. We are not achieving the energy savings we could. The program is allowing unjust operators to enter the field.
In my supplementary question I asked the minister to consider a special committee of this House. 1 ask that question again because 1 think a special committee would be able to take all the information which exists in the various departments. Right now not only is CMHC involved, but the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources are involved as well. A grouping of various departments and agencies is involved with home insulation.
I was suggesting that home insulation is very important to the country. It will save individual consumers as well as the country money. Why not set up a committee, bring the various departments together, have a thorough investigation of the existing practices, and come up with some new solutions? I suggest we bring the various departments, the research, the enforcement and the delivery of services-the three essential aspects to this program-together, and perhaps through a committee of this House offer to the government a new alternative on how this service, which is so essential to the Canadian people, can be delivered.

Mr. Speaker, first I want to thank my hon. friend opposite for his kindness in referring to the fact that I was here

October 29, 1979
Adjournment Debate
to continue this important debate with him tonight. It is a pleasure to do this because the hon. member is quite right that this is a very important topic. He is also quite right in saying that we inherited this problem from the former administration. That being the case, however, it is one which is very widely used. As a matter of interest, applications are coming in at about 10,000 per week. Approximately $60 million has been spent so far in 1979 on this program, but there are some administrative problems with it. There is no doubt about that, and I would not be prepared to dismiss out of hand the possibility of pursuing this by way of a committee along the lines the hon. member discussed.
However, I think it might be profitable first to discuss the matter in the regular standing committee to see what kind of information, debate and dialogue we can initiate there.
Questions about abuses are bound to occur with a program which is as widely used as this one. 1 am sorry that when the hon. member asked his question I did not make it clear that there are tests being done by the Ontario Research Foundation or other outside agencies on the basis of standards set by the Canadian Government Specification Board on other insulation products such as urea-formaldehyde. One of these tests is designed to ensure that the formaldehyde content does not exceed one part per million, which seems to me to be a pretty
exacting test. However, the difficulty that CMHC has had is that in administering the program for the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources it has had to rely on tests given to us by the Ontario Research Foundation.
We are now in the position with respect to cellulose insulation where, under the Hazardous Products Act, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Lawrence) can, as I understand it, order some of these products, if they are not accepted, to be taken off the shelves. I trust that there are other things we can do to improve the administration of this program. One of the things I am looking at-but in a tentative way at this point-is perhaps to combine this program with some other housing programs which have an energy factor in them.
In closing, CHIP is not a program which should be condemned out of hand simply because it is so widely used and there are many abuses reported. We have not been able to ascertain the actual extent of the abuses with any great precision as yet.
